    Chapter 19: Chapter 18

_/*Chapter 18:* / _

 

_/*Alexandria:* / _

It was easier, in that moment, to focus on the goings on in front of
her, easier to block out the eyes burning holes in the back of her head,
easier to push aside the knowledge that the /instant/ they had any
semblance of privacy a conversation /needed/ to be had.

She liked to think she avoided “easy.”. That she wasn’t afraid of doing
the hard things when they were needed. But for right now, she was
grateful for the temporary delay.

The ‘Mandalorians’ (as Rugess told her the armored terrorists were
called) –-- or what was left of them –-- were corralled by the police.
Most were unconscious, and would stay unconscious for a good /long/
while given their injuries. But a few were still aware enough.

Their helmets had been removed, their guns and backup auxiliaries as
well. The pile of wrist mounted flamethrowers, jetpacks, combat knives,
and such was impressive.

With their helmets off, Alexandria could see their faces, and, oh, what
a story she could read there.

They were angry – most of them anyway – resigned to their fate but proud
that they’d tried all the same. Not mercenaries then. Not hired thugs.
Those types didn’t feel /pride/. No. It was just a job.

This was /more/ than a job for them.

Ideologues. This was for a /cause/ of some kind.

Some looked at her, fearful and afraid, muttering under their breath
about “tech” or that she was a freak of some kind. Strictly speaking she
was, but that wasn’t relevant right now.

More than that a few kept looking around them, searching. /Expecting/
something. A second attack? Some kind of rescue?

She didn’t have enough information to tell. Not yet.

…

Perhaps she should have left more than two of the ground team members
aware and alert. The aggregate information might have been useful in
filling in the blanks.

“Excuse me.”

The voice brought Rebecca’s attention towards a man – a guard captain,
if she were judging the embroidery on his armor correctly compared to
his fellows – along with the woman behind him.

“I’m Captain Cadera of the Mandalore Royal Guard. This is Duchess Satine
Kryze of House Kryze.”

“I would like to extend my thanks for your timely intervention,” said
the woman. She was blonde, sharp featured; but wary, careful and on
guard. “Your display was… unique.”

Concerned. She was concerned.

Alexandria didn’t regret her display, not really. With no knowledge of
how Miss Militia’s fight was going in the ship, she needed to eliminate
the ground forces quickly in case her intervention was needed above.
And, if her powers were going to become known, she might as well use it
to get some clout with the local who merited an assassination /squadron/
to try and take her down.

Still, concern and fear were not ideal. But also not wholly unworkable.

“We’ve also received various statements from the passengers regarding
your compatriots,” Captain Cadera muttered, eyeing Miss Militia and
Clockblocker. “They say you… locked a man’s /boot/ to the deck?”

“We’re just full of surprises.” Dennis smiled, but it could barely be
called such. It was almost a sneer, and the expression sent alarm bells
flashing across Rebecca’s mind.

The boy was close to his proverbial limit. Whether it was seeing
Rebecca’s face and the associated pseudo-confirmation of the memories in
his head he seemed to dread, or the attack, or the situation in general
– or, more likely than not, a combination of everything she didn’t have
the time to discern right now – what she needed to do was make sure this
went over “well enough” to keep their doors of communication open.

“I understand if you have questions,” she cut in carefully, making her
voice sound softer as she watched the two. “We’ll be more than happy to
answer any of them, but it has been a very… trying trip. Might we
perhaps get treated for our injuries, rest and meet at your convenience
tomorrow?”

She watched the two of them carefully. Cadera looked to the Duchess,
waiting on her decision. Alexandria made certain to note that for the
future. He was loyal to the Duchess. She’d have to see if she could use
that in the future..

The Duchess herself was interesting. There was a slight narrowing of her
eyes that could be mistaken for her features softening as the rest of
her face did exactly that. She did feel indebted, and she understood and
agreed with Alexandria’s reasoning.

But she also knew she was being played.

She knew something wasn’t adding up here, with Alexandria herself.

Something she’d seen in the fight? Perhaps in Clockblocker or Militia’s
faces behind her? Or Rugess?

Regardless, the woman felt as though Alexandria was playing her false;
good instincts on the whole.

Then again, she was a duchess. Powerplays and false faces might very
well simply be par for the course.

“I understand and indeed, you should be allowed to rest.” The Duchess
nodded. “You are travelers, yes? Do you have accommodations for the
night? If not, the least I could do in repayment for your help would be
to offer you rooms in the palace.”

Alexandria hesitated. Satine’s expression told her the offer was, on the
whole, genuine. But the woman also wanted to keep them close in the way
one kept close a poisonous insect: so you wouldn’t lose it crawling
around the room.

Taking her offer had advantages, guaranteeing further conversation and
thus, room to manipulate an important ruling figure. But if the
conversation with Miss Militia and Dennis took a sour turn, which it
likely would, there might be far far too many eyes and ears overhearing
the contretemps for her liking.

Ruggess babbled something rapidly behind her. Vaguely, she recognized
his words as something positive about New Mandalorian Hospitality.

The Duchess seemed to take his words as accepting the invitation; she
smiled as she bowed ever so slightly. “Then I welcome you as guests of
House Kryze.”

Alexandria schooled her expression, wondering if she should argue
against it, the impending discussion with Militia and Clockblocker still
looming large in her mind, before she decided to avoid the awkwardness
of a refusal at this stage.

After all, if they went and found some sort of hotel, who’s to say the
Duchess wouldn’t simply have spies sent there?

It’s what she would have done in the Duchess’ place, at any rate.

(X)(X)(X)

Guards escorted them to the palace, driving them in a flying vehicle
bearing the sigil of house Kryze. The Duchess remained behind to keep
abreast of what the investigators found and to hear the information
extracted from the prisoners. That was fine; ideal, even. If she was
over there (along with whatever eyes-and-ears were dedicated to her
personal safety), she had, potentially, fewer eyes on them in her own
palace.

But the silence between the three Earthlings was /tense/ as they
traveled with the guards. A thousand questions brewed behind Miss
Militia’s eyes. Regarding her identity, regarding the betrayal of the
laws and ideals of the Protectorate and the PRT. The sense of betrayal /
Miss Militia /felt over the way the most obvious answers to these
questions trampled over everything she had thought they stood for was
almost plainly naked on her face.

A part of Alexandria felt genuine remorse for this turn of events. How
it would affect the way Miss Militia saw her. Her one-time Ward’s
admiration was something she’d never wanted to betray.

But more concerning was what she could see in the boy, Clockblocker.
He /stewed/ in his silence, bubbling like a simmering pressure cooker
ready to explode with every passing second. He was /seething/ in his
seat, and whatever thoughts were circling round and round in his head
were making it actively worse.

The grandeur of the palace was almost lost on them as they arrived,
preoccupied as they all were, but it was a /large/ structure. The Number
Man could have likely spent an hour measuring the place just by the size
of the doorway and the width of the halls.

The guards moved without a word of their own (save brief instructions
for places they could and could not go while they remained here), but,
even to them, it was obvious that their little group had far too much to
discuss, and they didn’t linger long past giving them the access codes
to their individual rooms.

She opened the doors to her room first, and both Miss Militia and Clock
forewent exploring their own spaces, rather choosing to follow after
her. Whatever conversation they were going to have about Rebecca Costa-
Brown, they were going to have it /right now/.

As she opened the door, the room was expansive: a large bed, a sitting
area, even a balcony; it would be considered a hotel VIP suite back
home. The square foot measure of Shmi’s entire house could fit just in
this room.

Alexandria used the space to gain some distance, stepping away from Miss
Militia and Clockblocker behind her. Rugess had been left with the
medics, finally getting his hands properly treated for the time being,
which granted them some much needed privacy.

“I take it you have questions,” she opened.

“Nah, seems really fucking clear to me.” Clockblocker’s voice came out
as a laugh, high in its pitch and high strung in its tone. Not quite
hysterics, but edging somewhere uncomfortably close to it.

“Dennis?” Miss Militia called, reaching hesitantly towards him.

But the boy brought his eyes up, staring at Alexandria with what was
undoubtedly /loathing/ in his gaze, disgust and anger and just the
faintest hint of desperation warring within them. “Tell me something,”
he chuckled. “Is this shit about Cauldron in my head real too?”

The way he said it was so /blasé/ - he said it so carelessly - that it
almost made her flinch. Her eyes flickered towards Militia, seeing the
confusion there.-

“Don’t say anything el-”

“Or what?” he laughed, and there was nothing /funny/ there, nothing
kind. The boy had reached the edge of his patience, reached the end of
his threshold of whatever it had been that had allowed him to hold onto
his composure until this moment.

It seemed, now that the worst of his fears were apparently confirmed,
that he was ready to let loose. “You’ll kill us?” he sneered as he
laughed again under his breath. “Not like any of us are in line for a
long and full life.”

“Dennis, stop.” Miss Militia was suddenly in front of the boy, hands on
his shoulders, forcing him to look at her and break his gaze away from
Alexandria. “You’re scaring me, what is this?”

The roiling, resentful anger frothing inside the boy seemed to calm, to
go still, even as he looked away from the both of them.

Then he spoke again, his voice softer this time but no less cutting.
“What is it, Chief Director? How much time do we have? Two years? Five,
tops? Those rumors make a lot more sense now. You knew. You must’ve
known how we’d all die-”

“Stop /talking/,” she barked, finding her voice, one of her fists
clenching tightly.

“_/*You*/_-” he snarled, face whipping back towards her in a rictus of
rage and hate that might have genuinely scared her had she been anyone
else. _/*“-don’t get to give me orders!”*/_

“STOP!” Miss Militia shouted, planting herself between Alexandria and
her Ward. “Both of you, /stop/! I don’t know what the /hell/ either of
you are going on about, but someone is going to give me answers and then
we’re going to /talk/ through this. Not scream at each other like idiots!”

“Scion is a ticking time bomb,” the boy blurted out, staring right at
Alexandria, /just/ to see if she would flinch. But she was ready, this
time; she didn’t. “In a few years, he’s set to go off. Kill everyone on
Earth. Me included.” He /chirped/ the last sentence, like someone
delivering a “neat” little factoid.

Miss Militia’s eyes widened, incredulity flashing there, and Rebecca saw
the opportunity for damage control.

“Your Ward has lost his mind,” she drawled, as calmly as she could force
herself to manage.

Dennis fixed his eyes on her again, and this time she felt the very real
need to brace herself.

“You die, drowning in /webs./”

She couldn’t help it, the memory /flashed/ before her mind, perfect
recollection allowing her to nearly physically relive the sickening,
horrifying sensation: chittering legs scratching at her throat,
mandibles biting at her tissues, muscles sucking down air that would not
come.

She flinched, and Miss Militia could see the truth of the words on
Alexandria’s own face, even if she wasn’t sure how to quite believe them.

Dennis marched across the room, nearly collapsing into a chair, as his
fingers rose to curl through his messy hair.

Silence drowned the room for several seconds.

“You weren’t surprised.”

It was Miss Militia who broke the quiet, her voice soft, almost
hesitating to do so. “I saw a lot of emotions on your face when we saw
Alexandria’s identity…” she confessed. “...but I didn’t see /surprise/.”

Dennis’s laugh sounded more like a sob this time.

The boy lifted his head. “I wanted to be wrong,” he whispered. “Because
if I was wrong about her identity, I could be wrong about everything
else I /remember/ too.”

He sucked down a shaking, broken breath of air, and this time he /was/
crying. The tears trailing down his cheeks also glimmered in his eyes as
he turned to look up at Miss Militia, pleading for some kind of
forgiveness. “But I wasn’t wrong,” he whispered, as though speaking his
words too loudly would make it all the more true.

He returned his gaze to Alexandria. “It’s all true, isn’t it? Everything
in my head. You, Legend, Eidolon. You guys are Cauldron. You gave out
powers, made the case 53s. Did you know? Did you know he’d eventually
kill us all?”

Miss Militia’s eyes darted to her, watching her, and Alexandria knew
that she could still /fight this/… she could still… salvage this.

She /could/ gaslight her, gaslight them both. On the face of it, what
Dennis was saying was crazy: conspiracy theories, raving about the end
of the world.

It may not be easy, but it /was/ doable. She would have to walk a very
fine line but…

A thought occurred to her then. A stray, /dangerous… /curiosity.

She paused, hesitating.

Then her hand reached down, towards the tablet they’d been using to
learn the language on the ship beforehand.

“Alexandria-”

“Give me…” she interrupted Miss Militia, fingers pausing, deathly still
over the screen, almost /afraid/ to touch it.

She didn’t. She realized…she /didn’t/ know. Hadn’t known.

She set the device down, backing away from it as she turned and stared
out of the balcony of their room to the city and deserts of Mandalore
beyond the glass..

But the thought, the /question/ of that insidious curiosity, had taken
root, writhing in her mind like a snake leaking poison from its fangs.

Silence reigned over them.

It was heavy. /Oppressive/. Suffocating almost as much as…

“Yes,” she finally said, the confession falling from her lips like a
lead weight. “It's true.”

She didn’t turn to look at Miss Militia’s face. She didn’t need to. The
betrayal she would find there was easy enough to predict.

“I became the Chief Director because we needed the world and the
Protectorate on the same page. Cauldron is an agency that sells powers
to both heroes and villains. Case 53s are a result of our experiments…
and we’ve been preparing for the inevitability of Scion’s rampage and
the extinction of humanity at his hands since the founding of the
Protectorate.”

Every word felt like a deathknell falling onto /their/ heads. Rarely did
Cauldron allow for anyone to know of who and what they were, let alone
the reality of Scion.

If not Contessa, then the Number Man would eliminate them. The more
people knew, the more his calculations could be thrown off, and the more
possibilities Scion could rampage early blossomed.

Even if she had wanted to, she wouldn’t have been able to protect them.
Not really.

/And yet…/ she wondered as her eyes trailed up towards the still orange
sky above.

/Did /any /of it… actually /matter/???/

The silence returned. A stillness in the room.

Miss Militia broke it. The only one here still… her. Still true and
almost /innocent/.

“We have to warn-”

“Warnings wouldn’t have mattered.” It was Dennis who interrupted Militia
this time. “There was nowhere to go. Nowhere to run… It wouldn’t have
mattered,” he muttered.

His thoughts were a grim echo to Alexandria’s own.

Miss Militia swallowed, clearly reeling with the revelations, before she
seemed to rally. She steadied herself and stepped forward to place her
hands on Dennis’ shoulders.

The boy didn’t look up.

“Dennis…” She swallowed again, her throat bobbing as she forced down
whatever doubts, whatever emotions threatened to reach up and silence
her. “We’re gonna figure this out… ok?”

Hopeful words. Pretty… but useless.

Were it so easy…

“Were they fighting?” Alexandria asked, perhaps choosing to stop the boy
from tossing Militia’s pretty words back in her face, or… perhaps… her
curiosity getting the better of her. “I know I was gone… but Eidolon,
Legend… Did we even slow him down?”

She didn’t get an answer, and that was answer enough.

Even so, she looked at him, hoping, fleetingly, that perhaps she might
be wrong.

Dennis gave her no such false hopes.

“He whispered something in Eidolon’s ear.” The boy shrugged. “Then he
killed him.” He stared her down, naked contempt in his eyes.

“So, congratulations… you bought us, like, ten minutes.” He stood from
his chair, marching towards the door.

“Hope it was worth it,” he said bitterly over his shoulder as he stepped
out of the room.

Alexandria waited until he was out of earshot.

“Follow him,” she demanded of Militia. “Don’t leave him alone.”

Her former Ward had too many questions, too many doubts. More than ever
before. But still, she followed /these /orders.

Not because she was compelled to, not because it was in her nature. But
because she saw the same thing Alexandria saw.

If they left the boy alone now, well… It was a tall building.

Miss Militia left. When Alexandria was alone, she fell into her chair.
She felt… heavy. Powerless.

Ten minutes.

The efforts of her entire life…

It all amounted to ten minutes?

 


    Chapter 20: Chapter 19

_/*Chapter 19:* / _

_/*Taylor:* / _

What I’d said felt like a confession: equal parts liberating as it was
horrifying. To tell someone, anyone, about this – even just a small part
of it – this cancerous, all encompassing /fear/ that now suffused my
life and sense of self…

Because that was the crux of the whole thing, wasn’t it:

Self.

I lost myself.

In truth, I’m still lost.

When I first woke… I wasn’t sure what of me /was/ me. If there was,
indeed, anything left of /me/.

When I realized I could move, that I could speak, I needed /someone/ to
know. For someone, anyone, to remember… /me/.

Not Skitter.

Not Weaver.

Not Khepri.

But /me./

Taylor.

I screamed my name, over and over again. I hadn’t even recognized that
it was Glory Girl, Victoria, at first. She was just /someone/… Someone
who could remember my name or even my face. Because I was sure to lose
it again in the next moment.

Only “the next moment” didn’t come.

Time passed, but I didn’t.

I didn’t fade away; or slip into the dark corners of my mind, the sense
of /me/ didn’t erode away like so much sand slipping through my fingers,
or like water through a net.

I remember it had felt so /impossible/ to hold onto /me/.

I huddled in the dark the first night, grasping the minds of hundreds of
millions of insects on Kashyyyk. Using their senses, their eyes and
their ears and their touch, to… watch me.

Because if I didn’t watch… I was so scared I’d simply fade into memory.

I didn’t sleep that night. Not out of fear… not immediately.

The fear came later.

I kept busy. Kept distracted. Hunted for food, tested the food on bugs
just in case Kashyyyk’s wildlife was poisonous.

When Vicky woke up the next morning, when she screamed at me, I remember
pulling back, retreating, not because of her or her voice… but rather
because – for a brief /horrifying/ instant – I wondered why I couldn’t
compel her to be silent and still.

I never wanted to think that again.

Listening to Vicky helped. Acting… with my own body, my own hands,
helped more. I had to remember. I had to remember that I had /hands/… I
hadn’t lost one. It was still mine. I’m still me.

The second night, I’d tried to sleep. I had. I’d been tired. The events
of the previous hours had left me drained and exhausted.

That’s when I grew afraid.

If I slept… would I wake up?

Would I wake up as /me/? Or as /her/?

I don’t know how I… escaped. How this happened.

What if it was all some strange dream? What if it all reset the moment I
closed my eyes for too long?

I feared my sleep. And when sleep finally caught up with me on the fifth
day, when I was too exhausted to keep my eyes open, that’s when the
nightmares came; or rather, the memories.

More vivid, more /real/ in my dreams than they were awake. The first
night I woke with a scream I choked off by biting down on my finger
until it bled

I was afraid… I was more afraid than I’d been in my entire life.

So, I forced myself to stay awake, using the tricks I… remembered… to
help push back the need to sleep for as long as I could.

But even that could only last for so long. I knew that. I knew I’d only
been forestalling the inevitable.

But, as /agonizing/ as it was, I kept pushing, kept trying, because
every second I was awake… It was another second where I was /me/.

I want to stay /me/.

When Vicky found me, after the celebration with the Wookiees, after my
body finally shut down and my eyes slipped closed…

I remember crying when I woke up. Partly out of the shock of waking up
at all, but mostly it was almost out of… joy. Or maybe, more fittingly,
relief.

I was still me. I was still… Taylor.

So when Vicky demanded I sleep, I didn’t have the will to resist further.

I’d fallen asleep – truly fallen asleep – /once/. So I could do it
again. The fear had diminished enough for that.

Even if the nightmares came, even if the memories that were mine and not
mine tore at me, I would sleep. Or try to, regardless. I made her
promise to wake me up if I had nightmares again. Because nightmares were
memories. If I was having them- then maybe I was slipping away again.

She promised. And that was enough.

I hadn’t expected to fall asleep for three days; but in hindsight, I
suppose I should have.

I’d been… very tired.

I hadn’t known what I expected when I woke up, but a little green priest
man was definitely not on the top of the list. Not even in the top fifty.

I’d been suspicious of Yoda, of course. I still was, to an extent.
Things like this… this… free charity, didn’t just /happen/. The
Wookiees, now the Jedi… were humans just so innately awful that aliens
were just better than us? More giving? Accepting?

That would just /figure/, wouldn’t it? That we’d be the only race that
had to be /forced/ to work together for survival.

…

…

I’d wanted to be wrong.

I sat in my room now, alone on the bed, the early risers of the temple
beginning their movements. Down one level, the young Padawan, barely a
month into her apprenticeship, was brewing tea for herself and her
Master, eager to begin “saber practice” today.

Two flights above, Jocasta Nu, the librarian woman that had been in the
Council Chambers, was speaking to the head of the ‘MedCorps’, trying to
fit myself and Victoria in for an examination and a suite of
vaccinations and cross-species antibacterials

Across the hall, two old Masters gathered in a community room to
continue their game of Dejarik, a chess game – or this Galaxy’s
equivalent. They each had a rule. Three moves, then continue the game
the next day. I wasn’t sure if they genuinely gave the game that much
thought or they used the near hour long “three moves” as an excuse to
gossip and chit-chat.

At the far end of my range, the kids, toddlers really, were being woken
up by their babysitters. Or teachers? Maybe. Not for the first time I
wondered where their parents were, or if this was some kind of boarding
school system and the kids would leave back home for the “summer” or
some such at one point or another.

Towards the other end I could hear gossip in the mess hall; apparently
an old Master, Dooku, had returned to the temple and it was causing a
stir. I’m fairly sure it was the old man I’d seen having a talk with
Yoda about his dead apprentice. I could see how that might bring someone
out of retirement.

But right across the door of my room, hovering, hesitating whether or
not to enter, was Vicky.

Finally, after almost a minute, I felt the deep breath she took through
the small gnat that was resting between her shoulder blades, squaring up
like she was getting ready for a fight before she… knocked on the door.

“Tay. I’m coming in, ok?” A pause. “Blink once for yes and twice for no.”

I did, in fact, blink, but in /confusion/.

Then I realized it was a joke.

The door whooshed open and Vicky was there, smiling a hesitant, awkward
smile at me.

“You ok to talk?” She asked.

I found myself raising an eyebrow. She’d been angry yesterday, I figured
she’d still be mad today.

I remembered, and yet /didn’t/ because it had /never happened,/ that
Lisa had once described Glory Girl as a bomb. Quick to go off, but once
the initial burst of anger was done, she was quick to move on.

She didn’t stew in it like I did, or my dad did. She didn’t nurse
grudges. Well, not /petty ones,/ anyway.

I offered a nod, still sitting quietly on my bed, the morning Coruscanti
sun beginning to cast shadows across my room.

She stepped forward and took a seat on my bed, near my legs hiding under
the comforter. I was a little caught off guard by the intrusion but not
quite enough to protest.

“I’ve been thinking about yesterday,” she started. “About what you said.”

That had been obvious enough. I’d been thinking about what I’d said
yesterday – and even what I hadn’t said.

“You–” She paused, seemingly trying to figure out a way to rephrase what
she’d been about to say, judging by her expression at any rate. “You
can’t… do this to yourself. I get being scared, but at some point you’re
gonna have to build a bridge and get over it.”

I snorted.

Were it so easy…

More than that, I wasn’t sure I wholly wanted to. Fear was another
distinction. Another thing that was just /me/.

Khepri never felt fear, not even in the worst of it. She was too lost
for that.

As cowardly… as /weak/ as it sounded, I’d rather live as myself with
fear, than as Khepri devoid of it.

Vicky set her jaw stubbornly at the sound, looking at me with something
I recognized – I’d seen it and /not seen it/ before. Not on her, but on
others. Defiant, who I’d never met, not truly. Chevalier. She looked
like she was getting ready to /save/ someone. Resolve in her eyes.

I didn’t /want/ or need her pity.

My hand, the one that shouldn’t be there and yet /was/ moved, plucking
the small datapad off my desk as I typed out a reply.

_/“I’ll cut you a deal/_.”

She perked up, and I almost felt guilty about it, about goading her,
giving her false hope.

_/“The day *you* remember, and *you* ‘build a bridge and get over it,’
I’ll do the same.”/ _

Her eyes shone with confusion for a moment, but then she grasped the
implications about /exactly/ how much I knew about her future and how
unpleasant it was.

I saw the sudden stiffening of her spine, the now-present trepidation,
before that stubborn squaring of her shoulders. That… /confidence/ that
let her think she was as /invulnerable/ as people thought she was.

I remember having that once.

I wanted to sneer, and I had to fight down the contempt I felt,
reminding myself that this wasn’t someone… making /light/ of this. Of
everything. But someone who genuinely didn’t know. That it was coming
from a place where she /thought/ she was helping.

And wasn’t that a twisted, horrid sort of irony too?

_/“Enough,”/_ I typed out. _/“Let’s get some food… talk about something
else.”/_

She still looked ready to argue, ready to push her point and insist,
before she thought better of it. “Alright,” she conceded with a nod,
though I knew this wouldn’t be the end of the discussion.

She got up off the bed, and there was a forced /lightness/ to her voice
as she spoke this time. Forcing herself to ignore the discussion she
wanted to have.

“I already showered so, you wanna do the same before we head out, or
would you rather grab breakfast first?”

A shower did sound good right now, a few more minutes of… /relative/
isolation before I stepped out into the temple full of mind readers and
empaths…

That was another headache. ‘The Force’

The more I listened in on the teachers, acolytes, Temple Guards, Jedi
and others in this temple, the more concerned I grew. This was the grab
bag of all grab bags and judging by the little display the Jedi Masters
put up, contacting our /passengers/ wasn’t beyond them either.

That /couldn’t happen/ with me. I wouldn’t /risk/ that… that /thing/
waking up.

I needed to learn more, find a way to at least /defend/ myself against
it, or confuse what they were sensing somehow.

Some of the quick Net searches I’d made - and had the service droid read
out to me because I couldn’t read “Galactic Basic” - told me that the
Jedi had fought many, /many/ wars in the past against regular non-force
users and lost. So that told me they could be beaten.

More than that, I’d already learned this temple had students who /
passed/ and /failed/ becoming Jedi.

Parahumans didn’t “pass or fail” using their powers. They simply did it.

Passing and failing implied this was a /skill/.

And skills could be learned.

As I gathered my clothes and let the warm water wash away the ever
present feeling of filth and blood on my flesh, my mind kept ticking
away as my bugs kept listening.

(X)(X)(X)

While we were getting ready to leave our rooms a few minutes later, as I
finished putting on the ‘slippers/shoes’ the Jedi had given us, I was
mildly surprised when someone knocked at our door.

“Hmm? Wonder who that is,” Vicky commented, stepping towards the door
and opening it.

“Greetings,” said the Jedi Master - the alien, Plo-Koon, if I remembered
correctly - bowing at the waist, hands clasped together, “and good
morning, Ms. Dallon, Ms. Hebert.”

“Oh, hello, Master…” I could see the moment that Vicky remembered she
didn’t /quite/ remember his name, and I felt a smirk tug at my lip as
she quickly pivoted onto the next subject. “What’s up?” she asked. “We
were just about to get something to eat. Does the Council need us?”

“No, I am not here on Council business, not strictly speaking, at
least,” he said. “I understand that your circumstances might make
acclimatizing to the temple somewhat difficult. If you like, I would be
willing to give you a tour of the temple grounds. I understand humans
dislike being confined to their rooms, and young humans even less so.”

“Oh! Well, that’s awesome! If it’s not a bother of course.”

“Never.” The alien shook his head. “I’d be pleased to help.”

I felt my eyes narrow, hackles rising.

What was his angle? I hadn’t heard anything through my bugs. Maybe he’d
been out of my range?

“I’d like that,” Vicky nodded, smiling brightly before turning to look
my way. “How bout you, Tay?”

I stared at her, my eyes shifting to the alien Jedi.

Slowly, I nodded, keeping my face carefully blank as I watched the
masked Master carefully.

“Wonderful,” Plo-Koon nodded. “Then I’d like to join you for the morning
meal, afterwards we can begin.”

“Sounds great,” Vicky smiled. “So… sorry if this is rude, but I’ve got
so many questions about… basically everything. What’s your species again?”

“Kel Dor.” The Jedi Master chuckled, stepping aside so Vicky and I could
walk out the door. “We come from the planet Dorin.”

“What’s the atmosphere there? Is that why you’re wearing a mask?”

I was reminded, somewhat distantly, of Vicky with the Wookiees.

I hoped the Jedi Master was as easy going as the big furballs and would
forgive what would likely be many, /many /upcoming “diplomatic-foot-in-
mouth” moments. Vicky was good at finding those.

 


    Chapter 21: Chapter 20

_/*Chapter 20:* / _

_/*Hannah:* / _

She followed after Dennis and (quite literally) jammed her foot in the
door as he tried to close it behind him, all but shoving the door open
after him. If he closed it, she didn’t have the code to get it back
open, and she was /not/ about to leave him alone to deal with… /
whatever/ all of this was.

“Dennis!” she called.

He stepped into his room, pausing at the spot between the entry and the
sitting area, head moving on a swivel, /searching/ for a distraction,
any distraction.

“Listen to me,” she pleaded softly, staring at his back. “Whatever this
is, whatever’s going on, you can talk to me. We can figure this out.”

“You know I’d really rather /not/ figure any more shit out right now,
Miss M.” His voice carried the sneer she couldn’t see as he turned
sharply to stalk off into the kitchen area. “I know, it’s against the /
rules /and all that, what with underage drinking, but seeing as how I
just got it confirmed I’ll be dying before I hit the legal age, I think
you can give me a hall pass for this one, eh?”

Was the question a distraction? Genuine? A mix of both? Her training and
experiences had covered emotional shock but it was too early to tell
just what pattern Dennis might fall into, if that’s even what this was.

“You’re angry,” she hedged on the safe bet. Anger was a default
response, a human ‘catch all’ safety net. Fear, sadness… those came
later. “I understand, I do, but–”

“No, you don’t!” he screamed, one hand punching the wall as he whirled
around to look at her.

Tears were in his eyes, streaming down his cheeks, his teeth bared in a
snarl; and there, slowly cracking through the anger was an unsettling… /
desperation/.

“What’s the last thing you remember?” he asked. “Before we came here.
What’s /the last thing/ you can think of?”

“I…” She hesitated, wondering if her answer, given all the context
she’d /gleaned/ from everything said so far, might make things worse…

Then she realized that Dennis might already know the answer, and getting
caught in a lie would be even worse at this juncture.

“I remember getting a call,” she admitted. “Lung. Armsmaster took down
Lung.”

“Yeah… Actually, not sure if that was total bullshit or not come to
think of it, but… /Good fucking times/.” He smiled, and there was
nothing kind about it, nothing easy or reassuring… there was nothing
of /Dennis/ in that smile.

It was all teeth, bitterness, spite and… /contempt/.

It worried her. It /scared/ her.

“Must be nice,” he laughed, “missing how everything went to shit, and
then kept /going to shit/!” His hand cut through the air, finger
pointing at her, as that desperate, manic anger reached a fever pitch,
trapped in the cage of his eyes.

“Bakuda, fucking Endbringers, the Slaughterhouse! Tohu, Bohu, Khonsu,”
he marked down the names like they should have meaning and she knew he
was getting angrier by the fact that they /didn’t/. She knew what some
were but it carried /weight/ with him. It carried memory. “Fucking Scion!”

She tried not to wince. For so long – the whole of her life, even –
Scion was a hero. /The/ Hero. The one who could save everyone, protect
anyone, and do anything.

For Dennis to believe… possibly to /know/ otherwise…

“The last thing I remember is him killing me. Killing /everyone./” The
heels of his palms dug into his eyes, as though physically trying to
shove back the tears. “I close my eyes and I see /gold,/ Miss M. I see
that beam coming at me! I hear the screams that just /stop/. I can’t get
it out of my fucking head!”

She stepped forward, her heart breaking for the boy that had apparently
been bottling up everything since they arrived, /hoping/ that something
would prove these memories, these beliefs, false – and had only found
confirmation.

Now that he had… he couldn’t bottle it up any longer.

He stepped away from her, keeping his distance; his eyes and face a
strange dichotomy of longing and disgust as he looked at her.

/“/_/*I wish*/_ I was like you!” he hissed. “I _/*wish*/_ I didn’t know
a fucking thing!”

She stepped forward, closer to him; it was a risk, she knew. He might
freeze her, then use the time to do… something she wouldn’t let him do
if she were aware, but she felt it was a necessary risk. Dennis /needed/
someone, anyone right now, not a woman who would treat him like a suspect.

“But you’re not,” she answered carefully, her hands slowly inching
forward to grab the boy’s biceps, squeezing in a way to reassure him
that he was /here/. With her. Not in a memory where he died. “You’re not
like me. And… I don’t want to tell you I know what you’re going through,
that I know what it’s like because I don’t. All I know is that you’re
strong enough to overcome this.”

“There’s no point,” he hissed, a blackness in his voice that unnerved
her, unsettling somewhere deep in the back of her mind. “There’s–”

“You are /alive/!” she cut him off, enunciating every word, hands
squeezing tightly. “You’re /here/! Whatever he did, whatever happened, /
you/ are _/*here*/_, Dennis! He /failed/.”

Dennis’s expression crumpled, the boy almost folding in on himself as
she closed the remaining distance and hugged him. He was still shorter
than her, his head just low enough to rest beneath her chin as she
squeezed her arms tightly around him.

“We’re alive for a reason, this happened for a /reason/.” she whispered,
feeling his hands digging into her back, holding onto her like a
drowning man grasping onto a life raft.

“Nothing could stop him,” Dennis sobbed. “Behemoth. Leviathan. He was
killing /Endbringers,/ Miss M.”

She felt a chill go down her spine.

She’d fought both those monsters at one occasion or another. She’d seen
what they could do.

If Scion could kill them…

She really wasn’t sure what chance any of them had.

But Dennis didn’t need to hear that. Didn’t need to be reminded of that.

“You’re not going to die again,” she answered him, praying somewhere
deep in her heart she wasn’t lying. “Whatever you saw, whatever you
remember… /just/ by us being here… it’s not the same anymore. We can
change it. We can fix things.”

“How?”

She had no idea.

She didn’t tell him that either.

Pulling away, she gently cupped the sides of his head in her hands,
making him look at her.

“I promise–” she answered quietly, “I /promise /that we’ll get home. And
when we do, we’ll bring back whatever we need to /win/.”

He didn’t believe her. She could see that.

She could also see that he wanted to. Desperately, fervently, he wanted to.

So he nodded… and he pretended.

She felt her heart break a little more at the sight.

(X)(X)(X)

She stayed with Dennis for a long, /long /while. He was exhausted and
drained, talking about what he remembered. Everything he could,
everything that /might/ be true, and might not be true.

If this was a fantasy, some shared delusion of some kind, it was
remarkably detailed and thorough.

Some things she wanted to push back against: the idea that Colin would
break the Endbringer Truce, or set some girl up to take the fall for him
out of spite.

She wanted to say that Piggot wouldn’t send children to fight the
Slaughterhouse Nine, let alone drop heavy ordnance right onto their
heads for the mere /chance/ to take out a member or two.

She wanted to believe that corruption didn’t run /so/ deep, couldn’t be
so systemic that not even Chevalier – bright, shining Chevalier – could
fix the organization. That he couldn’t even begin to truly grasp the
extent of the problem.

The people she worked with were better than that. The PRT was /supposed/
to be better than that.

And yet… evidence to the contrary was in the other room.

She didn’t want to leave Dennis alone, but the questions burned at her
mind. When the boy fell asleep in the living room chair from which he
told his story, she slipped out of the room.

Marching towards Alexandria now felt like marching to interrogate a
prisoner, and that thought was equal parts disturbing and dismaying.

When she reached the door, she entered the code that Alexandria had used
earlier, and the metal sheet slid sideways into the wall.

Alexandria was sitting almost in the exact same spot Hannah had left
her. She looked… exhausted. Leaning back in her seat, she had one hand
resting across her brow, and the other resting on the armrest.

She sat still as a statue, the gloom and dark of the Mandalorian night
casting the whole room in cold gray and unsettling hues of blue.

Hannah opened her mouth, ready to say… something. She wasn’t sure what,
when Alexandria beat her to it.

/“Meaningless/.”

She stopped, confused, almost unsure if she’d even /heard/ the whispered
word that slithered through the room like a malediction. “What?” She asked.

Alexandria shifted, the movement almost imperceptible and yet so very
unsettling for just how minute it was, like something chittering in the
dark and you weren’t sure if it’d moved at all.

“It was all… /meaningless/,” she repeated.

“What was?” Hannah asked, frowning as she stepped deeper into the room;
closer to her.

Silence reigned over the room for a long moment. The unsettling
stillness of Alexandria’s body was oppressive, like a high pitched note
growing louder in the back of her mind.

“We had projections,” Alexandria finally said. “Precogs. Thinkers. We
didn’t know the exact numbers. But we knew how many we’d lose… more or
less. Lowest estimates, the optimistic ones, were five-hundred billion.
Higher ones were in the hundreds of trillions.”

Militia wondered for a moment how that made sense, knowing there were
less than six billion on earth.

Then she remembered that there were other worlds. Earth Aleph for
instance. And even more besides that.

Add enough of those planets together… you could reach those numbers.

Would Scion have wiped them /all /out?

Why?

“Do you know how many humans live in this galaxy, Militia?” Alexandria
asked and Hannah’s eyes darted towards the tablet resting on the coffee
table right in front of Alexandria, though its screen was now dark, like
the rest of the room.

Her eyes returned to Alexandria, finding the woman’s own gaze fixed on a
spot somewhere on the table. Staring far away, staring past the room,
staring past Hannah herself.

“The minimum number is nearly seven quadrillion…” She snorted. “Last
they checked.”

Hannah wasn’t sure what to say to that.

“The attack can happen,” Alexandria continued. Somehow, Hannah
understood that she was no longer talking to her, not really. “He can
kill… everyone… And it wouldn’t have wiped us out. Humanity would have
lived on. We’d still exist.

“All of it…” Alexandria /shuddered/. “It was always… pointless.”

Hannah stood there in the darkened room, feeling uneasy. Out of place.
Seemingly in an eyeblink both her Ward and her mentor were suddenly off
their respective centers, despairing in equal if different ways.

She’d never seen Alexandria like this, not even in the worst of times,
after the most devastating of defeats. But now…

She moved softly, quietly, as though afraid to disturb the stillness of
the room.

She took a seat on the couch beside Alexandria’s seat. Her knees felt
stiff, and her throat dry. Armsmaster said she was good with people;
right now she wished that were true.

“You’re a good person,” she decided to say.

Alexandria snorted dismissively, almost disdaining. “You don’t know /
nearly/ enough to say that. You’re saying it to make /yourself/ feel
better, because otherwise you were taught by a false hero, and just what
does that say about /you/.” she replied, speaking with a coldness and
sharp, cutting certainty that had always made Hannah both admire and
fear her judgment as a child.

But right now, she felt her hackles rise, anger bubbling under the surface.

It was one thing to make mistakes. It was entirely a different matter to
refuse to correct it if you could.

Alexandria had been the one to teach her that.

“You were a real hero once!” she retorted, heat entering her voice. “Do
you still want to be one? Or would you rather be… /this/!”

There was no denying that Alexandria had grown colder, harsher, more
severe and more demanding since Hannah had first trained under her, all
those years ago.

Hero’s death, the Siberian, Behemoth, Leviathan and the Simurgh, each of
these had taken their toll, making her harder. And now, seemingly, Scion
as well bore down on her shoulders. Had always been bearing down on her
shoulders.

Hannah could understand why Alexandria’s idealism might have died. She
could /forgive/ the fact that her mentor might have become something she
once would have fought against.

But only if Alexandria herself wanted to change, this time for the better.

The woman watched her now, as if studying a canvas. With her usually
helmet-obscured face naked, Hannah could almost read Alexandria’s own
bared “micro expressions”, subtle as they were.

Hannah shook her head. “Maybe you lost your way. Maybe things went
wrong, or… whatever. But you’re still alive. You and Dennis… this gives
you a /chance,/ now.”

“We /lost,/ Militia,” Alexandria sighed. The word ‘lost’ was pronounced
like a damning condemnation. “Everything we did – everything _/I/_ did –
I could live with. I’d do it all again, if it meant that we won! But… /
ten minutes./”

She never screamed. She never raised her voice. But the severity, the /
emotion/, was certainly there.

Alexandria shook her head with a laugh filled with bitterness and
sorrow. /“Ten minutes/…”

Before she knew what she was doing, Hannah had closed the distance,
shuffling forward to place her hands on Alexandria’s shoulders as she
had for Dennis before her, standing over the sitting heroine in a way
that she never would have thought would happen, their roles utterly
reversed.

“What happened, /happened/,” she shook her head. “We don’t know how we
got here. Maybe that can’t be changed. Maybe it can. But regardless of
whether or not /that/ can change, what /can/ change is how you do things
now. How you do things going forward.”

“...Even if I tried… I’m not sure I’m able anymore.”

“Why not?” Hannah felt like she was talking someone off the ledge of a
building, their feet standing at the edge of the drop.

Alexandria looked up at her and, in the dim light of the room, her false
eye caught the light, its glass reflecting the cold blue almost like a
cat’s.

“That woman died,” she finally whispered softly. “I’m not sure when… All
you’re looking at is the corpse… puppeted by whatever’s left to be in
control”.

“I don’t want to believe that,” the younger woman answered firmly. “The
woman who made me who I am today is no more dead than I am.”

Alexandria shook her head. “You’re a good woman… a good hero. You don’t
need validation from a creature like me.”

“Maybe not.” Hannah shrugged. “Validation isn’t what I’m looking for. I
just want to help you. Both of you. I may not remember anything, or know
everything. But somehow, right now, I think the both of you could
actually use that.”


    Chapter 22: Chapter 21

_/*Chapter 21:* / _

 

_/*Anakin:* / _

Anakin felt, frankly, conflicted about Master Yan Dooku.

On one hand, when he was younger, in his imaginings of the Jedi from the
stories, Master Dooku was probably someone he could have pictured in
those more innocent days of his life.

Tall, dressed with an air of regality and… /command/. As though his
voice alone could demand the /galaxy/ bend the knee and it would be /
compelled/ to do so.

He /felt/ like a Jedi _/*Master*/_.

On the other hand, viewing Master Dooku with such awe felt almost like
a /betrayal/ of the man who was his actual Master, Obi-Wan.

And Anakin /did /still consider Obi-Wan his Master, because without Qui-
Gon and subsequently Obi-Wan, the boy doubted he would even be in the
Temple, let alone a Padawan learner.

Anakin also found himself resenting Master Dooku for the unwelcome way
he upset the status quo. Anakin had just begun to settle in, to know
Obi-Wan's tells and habits, how his Master taught lessons or approached
certain discussions.

Now that was thrown out the proverbial window. Not just because Dooku’s
way of teaching was very, /very/ different as far as Anakin could tell –
far more rigid and far more demanding – but also because Obi-Wan himself
was acting differently now that Dooku was here. It was throwing Anakin’s
tenuous new normal off, and he didn’t like it.

Still, today was supposedly saber practice, something Anakin could take
some measure of relief in. The physical training and art of meeting an
opponent blade to blade was always exhilarating. And supposedly Master
Dooku was no slouch in that regard, so perhaps the uncomfortable
juxtaposition of awe and resentment for the older Jedi Master could
resolve itself a bit, if only for the duration of this lesson.

So today would hopefully make a lot of these issues… worth it.

Entering their usual training rooms, Anakin wasn’t surprised to find
that Obi-Wan was not yet present; he usually took a few minutes longer
than Anakin did to arrive at saber practice, probably to teach his
Padawan patience, if he were any judge on Obi-Wan’s thinking.

He was surprised – at least a little bit – however, to find Dooku in the
training room, sitting on one of the side benches.

The old Master seemed to be meditating to pass the time while he waited,
eyes closed, back straight. Anakin noticed, of course, the peculiar
curved hilt of the lightsaber at the Master's waist.

The design was curious and unique. He’d never seen a curved lightsaber
before. He didn’t even know they could /be/ curved. Why didn’t the other
Masters have curved hilts? Was it some kind of status symbol? Had Dooku
been Battle Master before Cin Drallig? If so, why didn’t Cin have a
curved hilt saber?

“It is rude to /stare, /young Skywalker.”

Anakin almost jumped out of his skin at the man’s voice, looking up to
find the old man’s eyes now open and staring at him. “Ahh, sorry, Master
Dooku,” he stammered.

The Master did little more than make a sound in acknowledgement to the
words. “Kenobi?”

It took him a second to realize Dooku was asking where Obi-Wan was. “Oh,
I usually show up a bit earlier than Master Obi-Wan, start preparing
some of the training equipment, make sure the room isn’t occupied or set
to be used by other Masters and Padawans.”

“Hmmm,” Dooku made another acknowledging sound, but commented no further.

Awkward silence beginning to descend, Anakin decided to simply /ask/
what was on his mind.

“Why is your lightsaber curved?”

In answer, Dooku raised a slender eyebrow. “I take it then, that neither
you nor Obi-Wan have read Master /Skarch Vaunk’s /extensive treatise on
the seven forms.”

/Ehhh… Master who now?/

His answer must have been writ large across his whole face. Dooku
snorted, though there was no… /increased/ disapproval, just that same
general air that he’d always carried that said that whatever was in
front of him was found wanting.

“Qui-Gon was talented, but was always more interested in the intricacies
of the Force, especially the Living Force,” Dooku continued. “I suppose
I shouldn’t be surprised he didn’t put much emphasis on the forms,
especially after Xanatos.”

Anakin wasn’t sure what to say to that. In truth, he was fairly sure
Dooku was talking more to himself than to him.

As if to save him from awkwardness, the door hissed open and Obi-Wan was
suddenly there. His /true/ Master blinked curiously as he caught sight
of the two of them. “Anakin,” he acknowledged his apprentice. “Master
Dooku, I wasn’t aware you’d be so early in joining us. We haven’t even
done our usual warm up exercises.”

“Nor will you,” Dooku answered brusquely, and Anakin felt his
expectations fall down to his feet.

He knew that tone.

“It seems we will have to begin with the fundamentals.”

Oh boy…

Obi-Wan’s lips pursed /ever/ so slightly. “Master, I can assure you,
that isn’t necessary. The fundamentals of saber combat are known to me,
and setting Anakin back even further in his studies will not only hurt
him, but dismiss the tremendous effort he’s already placed in catching
up with his peers.”

A part of Anakin was touched that Obi-Wan had even noticed that. The
other part of him wished to loudly state /‘leave me out of this’. /

“I was unaware Jedi training was a /contest/,” Dooku huffed. “Skywalker
will ‘catch up’ on his own time. Training and teaching will not be /
rushed/. One must /meet/ standards, not simply pay lip service to them.”

Obi-Wan still seemed rather displeased. “I assure you, Master, our
training has not been sub-par.”

Dooku raised a slender eyebrow.

Reaching gently with his hand, Anakin could feel the eddies of the Force
flowing out of the Master. Two training sabers rose from their cradles
on the rack and glided into position between Obi-Wan and Dooku.

“Take hold of your weapon,” Dooku commanded, grasping the hilt of the
training saber, holding the weapon loosely with one hand. “Should you
still have hold of it by the seventh exchange, I will rescind my plans
for training and yield to your wishes.”

Obi-Wan looked unsure but then, with a furrowed brow and a look of
determination, grabbed hold of the blade.

As the first Jedi to have slain a Sith in over a thousand years, Anakin
expected the duel to be an exciting one. He expected that if Obi-Wan
couldn’t win, then he could at least hold his own for a while. Dooku had
only challenged him to seven exchanges. Even Anakin tended to last
against Obi-Wan for at least ten when they practiced before he made a
mistake.

It lasted four.

As Dooku plucked Obi-Wan’s falling saber out of the air with negligent
ease, the old Master raised a droll, slender eyebrow.

“We will begin with Master /Skarch Vaunk’s /treaties regarding the seven
disciplines… immediately,” he stated to the stunned duo.

(X)(X)(X)

_/*Master Plo Koon:* / _

Plo Koon didn’t consider himself /old/, not by the standards of his
people, and certainly not by the standards of the multi-species Jedi Order.

But after spending the early morning hours with the two humans, he felt
almost wizened when exposed to the blinding radiance of Ms. Dallon’s
enthusiasm and ceaseless curiosity. Like a child, with eyes full of
wonder at the discovery of so very many new things.

It was a stark contrast to Ms. Hebert, who played the placid and calm
moon to Ms. Dallon’s shining, incandescent sunlight.

Considering her mood just yesterday during the Council meeting, the
drastic change was almost startling.

But, beneath the surface he could sense Ms. Dallon’s turmoil. The raging
tempest of emotion and confusion had been suppressed, but it wasn’t
gone. Not at all.

That suppression concerned him. They were not Jedi. As such, releasing
their emotions into the Force wasn’t a practice either of them used, and
everything he knew about humans told him this was… problematic.

But he also knew simply confronting her with those emotions might cause
more harm than good.

And so even as he spoke, he was trapped in something of a conundrum: to
allow the girl her distractions (as was no doubt comfortable for her),
or to attempt to help her as his conscience dictated he try, perhaps to
help all /three/ of them – the young women, and the Fragile One..

“So wait, those eye lenses aren’t to help you see, but because if you
didn’t have them your /eyes /would melt!?” Ms. Dallon’s eyes were wide,
inching forward as if she could peek through the black lenses to look at
his “melting eyes”.

“The fluids would evaporate,” he clarified, chuckling. “Melting and
evaporating are two different things.”

“Right, right, sorry,” she answered absently, still staring a little
wide eyed at him and his lenses.

They were in the hanging gardens now, where the Coruscanti sun warmed
the peaceful boughs and pathways. Padawans and Knights moved quietly
along the paths, either towards their training, their lessons, or simply
enjoying the serenity for themselves.

“Your home-” he decided to ask, sidestepping her fascination. “You told
us there were many like you and Ms. Hebert. Parahumans?”

She went to nod, then hesitated. “Well… /many/ is… kind of relative now
that I think about it?” One hand rose, finger scratching at her cheek.
“Like, last I checked there were about /maybe/ a hundred thousand
parahumans world wide? When compared to the Jedi or everything that must
be in this galaxy… doesn’t seem like a lot.”

“The Jedi of today do not number a hundred thousand, but I take your
meaning.” A curious thought entered his mind at his own statement, but
it was a curiosity to look into later. “But one thing confused me: you
mentioned groups of parahumans that were enemies would band together to
fight greater dangers. The ‘Endbringers’, if I recall.”

“That’s how it went,” she nodded.

“You had a common enemy, an alliance of convenience… but that enemy was
never defeated. Would their efforts not have been better served
attempting more… long term cooperation in order to achieve a victory?”

The answer didn’t come from Ms. Dallon, but rather as a derisive, /
contemptuous/ snort from Ms. Hebert that drew both of their respective
attentions to her.

She didn’t quail under the attention, staring at both Ms. Dallon and Plo
Koon himself as if daring to contradict her.

_/*“People don’t cooperate,*/_” The insects hissed and chittered around
them.

As it had done in the Council Chambers, it gave the air of the gardens a
singular /crawling/ effect.

_/*“They’re selfish and stupid. You either force them to work together,
or they’ll all burn to death pushing and shoving to crawl out the door*/_.”

Even without a voice, the answer was delivered with such anger, such /
rage,/ that it told Master Plo Koon that these words were backed with
the bite of /experience/.

“That can be true at times-” He replied carefully, gauging her reaction
as he did. It wasn’t even a lie either. People of all corners of the
galaxy could be foolish and selfish. “-but people can be reasoned with.”

She offered another snort through her nostrils, disagreeing again. It
was… heartbreaking almost, for one so young to be so jaded.

Curiously, however, he saw Ms. Dallon’s expression take on a calculating
veneer, the wheels of her mind clearly turning on an idea.

“Hey, Master Plo.”

“Hmm?” he asked, genuinely curious.

“You’re a Jedi Master Like Yoda, Mrs. Yoda and the others, right?”

Plo Koon tried very hard not to choke on his own breathing.

Mrs. Yoda?

No doubt she was talking about Yaddle.

“Yes, I am, bu-”

“Great!” She smiled, interrupting him mid correction. “So… I’m
wondering- I know /you/ guys can talk to… Fragile One, but is it
possible for me to talk to… it? Is it an it? A her? I hope it's not a
he. I don’t want a guy in my head.”

If Plo Koon had eyebrows, one would be raised right now.

Sharp spikes of nervousness flashed like knives across his senses. Ms.
Hebert's was serrated with fear and concern. Dallon’s was thin, like the
point of a needle.

But he could feel Ms. Dallon's determination as well; pulled from the
forge of her spirit, like steel quenching in cold waters, hardening as
it took sudden shape in her mind.

“It… /might/ be possible,” he stated slowly.

She smiled. “Grea-”

“But-” he interrupted, one hand rising to halt her enthusiasm. He
realized, somewhat distantly, that this might be quite necessary when
dealing with Ms. Dallon in a very general sense. “I must ask: Why?
Yesterday, you were quite dismayed.”

He didn’t miss the quick look towards Ms. Hebert out of the corner of
Ms. Dallon’s eye before she looked at him, spine straightening.

“I think I gotta make sure it’s not dangerous, right?”

Before he could answer, Hebert grabbed hold of the other girl’s arm,
pulling her so she’d turn to face her completely.

_/*“Don’t.*/_”

Ms. Dallon frowned, crossing her arms. “Look Tay… It’s not /going/
anywhere.”

_/*“You’re being an idiot-”* / _

“Probably,” she shot back with a shrug. “But like I said. It’s /here,/
it’s /staying,/ and if it’s gonna be dangerous or /helpful/ I’d like to
know. I mean, hell, Master Windu said it was /devoted/ to me. That has
to count for something!”

Plo Koon watched, listening carefully. Many would be surprised by how
much they could discover when they simply stopped and /listened. /

The unspeaking girl’s left hand clenched tightly into a fist, almost as
tight as the knot of rage and genuine worry coiling within her like a
pit of serpents.

“Ms. Hebert,” he carefully interrupted, her attention snapping to him
with a withering glare, as though /he/ were at fault for this. “I
understand you’re… reluctant to speak on these entities, but perhaps
some insight might make this safer for Ms. Dallon, if she’s intent on
following through with this?”

_/*“You-”*/_ The bugs hissed and her overwhelming /presence/ sent many
of the nearby Knights and Padawans flinching at the cold icepick across
their senses. _/*“-can just say, ‘No!’”*/_

The insects of the garden were growing agitated, so much that the
tension was now being actively noticed by those around them.

He raised his hands.

“If you are so adamant, I will respect that,” he answered carefully,
already seeing Ms. Dallon’s cheeks puffing up, ready to argue. “But,” he
paused for effect, “other Masters might not. The need for knowledge of
what we’re dealing with, confirmation of the danger or opportunities
they pose…, even mere curiosity. It may also be the only way to find
your way home.”

“And besides,” Ms. Dallon pulled her arm free of Ms. Hebert’s grip, the
two girls glaring at each other, “you’re not the boss of me.” She glared
a challenge at the dour girl.

“She merely speaks out of concern,” Plo Koon interjected, for the first
time stepping forward to interpose his hand between the two young women.
Ms. Dallon, as he noted before, was like fire. Her emotions were bright
and brilliant. But fire burnt itself out quickly.

Ms. Hebert was far different.

But /both/ were headstrong. Proud. Used to getting their way. Ms. Dallon
by the force of her personality, Ms. Hebert by… /force/.

And here, when both were acting out of /concern/ for the other, neither
wanted to have the other get in the way.

Perhaps later they might laugh at this.

Right now was not that time.

“Let us revisit the discussion at a later time,” he suggested, though
both girls kept glaring at each other. No doubt they would be speaking
at length, /privately,/ about this. “Allow tempers to cool.”

Ms. Dallon huffed, “/Fine/.”

Ms. Hebert turned away.

Hmmm. Crisis averted, he supposed.

(X)(X)(X)

_/*Obi-Wan* / _

He’d always believed, as perhaps all Knights and Padawans believed, that
he was good at lightsaber combat. Perhaps not a /master/, but at the
absolute least, he was /good/ at it.

Four exchanges with Master Dooku.

That’s all he lasted.

The Master had made it look so /easy,/ like it wasn’t even an /
afterthought/ to him. A deft movement here, a parry there, a thrust and
the next thing he knew his practice saber was out of his hand.

Now, though, Master Dooku was sitting Obi-Wan and Anakin down in the
library and dictating a lesson plan involving treatise after treatise,
book after book on the philosophy and theory of lightsaber combat. /Theory/!

He wasn’t a creche youngling.

Still, apparently, it had yielded results for Master Dooku, if his
stunning skill with the saber was any indication.

And /that/ bade another question to worm its way into his mind.
Squirming, insistent, and demanding he voice it as Anakin looked at the
list of prescribed reading material with a barely hidden /dismay/. No
doubt his Padawan wanted /practical/ lessons.

He wasn’t sure if that would make him slower, or would make him force
himself to chew through the material so he could get back to the
physical practice all the quicker.

“Is this everything?” Anakin asked.

“For now,” Dooku answered drolly. “When we reconvene in three days,
answer seven of my questions – one from each tome – correctly, and we
will begin with proper saber training.

The lines on Anakin’s face hardened, determination entering his
features, and Obi-Wan was fairly sure he had his answer to his previous
question.

Grabbing his datapad, the boy stood and started walking out, tossing a
curious look over his shoulder as Obi-Wan lingered behind.

The Knight smiled at his Padawan. “Go along, Anakin, I’ll just be a
moment with Master Dooku.”

The young boy shrugged, nodding before heading off.

As the door hissed shut behind him, Dooku was the one who spoke first.

“You have a question.”

It was an observation. A correct one.

“Why didn’t you train Master Qui-Gon this way?”

If Master Qui-gon had a fraction of Dooku’s mastery over the saber… maybe-

“What makes you believe I did not?”

Dooku’s voice was calm, the deep baritone burr of it rolling across the
training room as he turned his head ever so slightly to look at Obi-Wan
out of the corner of his eye.

But Obi-Wan wouldn’t back down. Crossing his arms he forced himself to
remain equally calm, reminding himself that he wasn’t /accusing/ Dooku
of anything…

“Master Qui-Gon didn’t wield the blade as you do. I don’t recognize
anything of your style in his Ataru, nor any of his Ataru in your own
form, brief as the encounter was.”

“Hmmm.” The sound Dooku made this time was faintly approving.

The old Master drew his lightsaber hilt, holding it up in the palm of
his hand.

“What is this weapon, young Kenobi?” Dooku asked.

“A Jedi’s lightsaber is his life.” The words rolled off his tongue
automatically, rote and succinct.

“Hmpf,” Dooku scoffed. “I always told him that… in a sense, it still
holds true. But I fear my Padawan never truly internalized it. Tell me:
do you know – do you /understand –/ what those words /mean,/ Kenobi?”

Obi-Wan raised an eyebrow, gaze trailing down towards the unique, almost
beautiful design of Dooku’s curved saber hilt.

“A Jedi who loses his lightsaber… will likely die shortly thereafter.
The saber is the direct, physical representation of his connection to
the Force. It, in a sense, guards and represents his life.”

“Hmm.” Dooku shook his head. “An answer, but an incomplete one, Kenobi.”

“In what way?” he asked, almost challenged.

Dooku obliged him. “What this weapon /is/, is the Jedi’s /life/. Travel
anywhere in the galaxy, and they may not recognize the robes. They may
not recognize the words or the unnatural tranquility… but they /will/
recognize this.”

He lit the blade, the blue glow suffusing the space between them, the
gentle hum filling the silence.

“Its design is /yours/. Unique to the hands that built it. Its scars are
the tapestry of the worlds and dangers the Jedi has faced. The glow of
its light, the peace and hope of the people saved by its blade, the hum
of its voice, the last sound heard by those it has felled defending the
people of the galaxy. The touch of the Force is the mural that tells the
tale of the mark left by its Jedi upon the galaxy and the Force itself.
This weapon /is/ your life. It will outlive you. It will outlast you,
and eventually it will /carry/ you long after you are gone, as we must
all go one day, Kenobi.”

Obi-Wan didn’t know what to say to that. It was clear Dooku had thought
long and hard regarding this, or perhaps the books he’d assigned them to
read carried more weight than his datapad could properly convey.

Dooku straightened, the blade shutting off, the hilt returning to its
hook on the old Master’s belt. “Qui-Gon did not take to the blade; that
was his choice, and I respected that choice. His pursuit of knowledge of
the Living Force made him a wise man. A good Jedi. Better than I. Even
so, I wonder now if I erred in my indulgence of his wishes.”

“You didn’t,” Obi-Wan answered automatically. Qui-Gon’s death hurt, it /
still/ hurt. And of course that very question had been what had started
this conversation in the first place. But letting his Master’s Master
stew in such regret seemed… needlessly cruel.

“Regardless…” Dooku pushed on, “the past is the past, and I will not be
repeating this error with you or Skywalker. Whether the Sith have truly
returned, or you killed the last of them, you will learn and you will
learn /well/, even if you hate every moment of it.”

“Jedi do not hate,” Obi-Wan answered automatically, rote and succinct,
and he suddenly wondered if his reflexive response was as lacking as his
saber answer had been.

Apparently, it was.

Dooku snorted. “There is /much/ for you to learn, indeed.”
