_/*Dennis:* / _

“Is this it?” Hannah asked, eyeing the picture on the dataslate,
comparing it against the building in front of them.

He couldn’t blame her for the question. The picture seemed to have been
taken at night, with the shop lit up in bright neon colors and moving
holo images. In the daylight, this place looked tame by comparison.

Still… “The sign matches,” he said, shrugging.

Hannah squinted, looking over the letters. The written characters of
Galactic Basic were still strange to both of them, even after the last
couple of years, and it took them time to read them properly.

Eventually, though, she seemed to agree with his assessment. Collapsing
the dataslate and stuffing it into her pocket, she marched forward to
head on in.

He followed after her, and a little chime played when the door whooshed
open, the local equivalent to a bell hanging overhead to rattle by the door.

‘Hello?” Hannah called, stepping inside. Dennis cast his eyes around the
little shop. He recognized some things here: smoking pipes, bongs – or
at least the local equivalents. Apparently, stoners were everywhere.

Some things, he /didn’t/ recognize. He supposed they were the equivalent
pieces for alien physiology, but they could be bombs for all he knew.
There was still so much he didn’t know about this galaxy, even after all
his time spent traveling.

“Hello!?” Hannah called again, and the lack of answer a second time made
him start to worry.

Hannah tossed him a look, but still didn’t draw a gun. The green energy
by her hip remained a blade, little more than a combat knife.

She stepped past the front counter, towards a back room. “Hello, we’re
looking fo-”

The knife at her hip was suddenly in her hand; then it was a small hand
cannon.

His own hand went to his blaster.

“Call the Count,” Hannah demanded, not looking his way.

He inched forward, peeking past her shoulder to see a very /dead/ Rodian.

“Shit,” he cursed. “Don’t suppose you know the time for rigor to set in
for Rodians?”

She shook her head. “No. But my guess, an hour or two, tops.” She
pointed, and on the floor he saw a long pipe of some kind. Smoke was
still wafting from its cup.

He reached down to his waist, plucking free his full helmet and shoving
it onto his head. “Let’s go. I’d rather the local cops didn’t exactly
find us with the dead guy.”

Hannah agreed, though he saw the moment of hesitation, the instant where
she had to remember she /wasn’t/ in Protectorate anymore, and this
wasn’t the US. He didn’t know how Utapau treated its criminal suspects
and, if possible, he’d rather avoid finding out.

“Let me take some pictures of the scene,” she suggested suddenly. “There
might be something the Count sees that we don’t.”

Not a bad idea. “Alright, I’ll wait outside. Let’s leave quickly.”

She didn’t like it, but she didn’t contest. They’d call Utapau security
later, when he was back on his ship and with the Count, who had some
pull for being a Jedi. Or, well… /a Count. /But /not /here, isolated
from any social or political support.

The door to the outside whooshed open, and Dennis was knocked flat on
his ass as a blaster shot smashed into his helmet. His head rang and the
world spun as he crashed into some display cases behind him.

“Dennis!” he heard Miss Militia scream through the ringing in his ears.

He didn’t have beskar. He’d never joined any clan. But Mandalorians made
good armor, so the shot that should have been fatal merely scored a deep
gouge across his helmet’s crown. Before any more shots could fire
through the door, he was stumbling and rolling his ass behind cover!

He pressed his back against the wall, the spike of adrenaline sending a
tingling through his fingers. His breathing was sharp and rapid, his
chest rising and falling quickly, and yet not enough air was coming into
fuel his racing heart as his shaking fingers took firm hold of his blaster.

He heard screams outside, the rapid pounding of feet as hundreds ran
away from the shooter.

/“Ya know, I thought you’d be a tougher contract, Kronos.”/

His breath stilled, as his gaze turned to Miss Militia, who was equally
wide eyed at that.

The shooter was here for /him/?

How?

“Didn’t know I had admirers,” he answered back, if only to fill the
silence and center himself.

“Oh, you’ve got plenty. Enough for them to foot the bill for the Bando
Gora to come after you.”

Chatty. That was good. He needed chatty right now.

He shifted his arm, just a bit. The warped reflection of the silvery
metal plate let him see around his cover without exposing too much of
himself.

Three, four, six. Six men.

He made a signal towards Militia, falling back on that old Wards/
Protectorate signal system he’d memorized all those years ago.

Six minimum, confirmed.

She nodded.

“Never heard of ya,” he answered. “But you must be worth something; how
the hell’d you find me here? /I/ didn’t even know I’d be here!”

That’s the part that was most concerning. Of course he had enemies. /
Lots/ of enemies. Jabba the Hutt on Tatooine had sworn he’d see him
boiled alive for that run where he had freed seven hundred slaves from a
single bulk shipment (they stopped sending shipments that size, now;
shame). He could see them hiring hitmen to kill him. But Utapau wasn’t
anywhere near his usual stops. And this shop wasn’t even known to him
until a few hours ago.

So how in fuck!?

“Sorry, kid, secrets of the trade. Now, you gonna be a good sport and
make my job easy?”

“Nah,” he called. “Hard way’s more fun!”

He /chucked /something out the door.

“Grenade!” Someone shouted.

/“Note to self,”/ he thought as he rushed out the door, /“Keep actual
grenades on hand.”/

The small container of fragrance oils shattered against the cover the
hitmen were hiding behind, and by the time they realized the deception
and moved to point at him again, the rather large welcome mat he’d
picked up from the floor was now a timelocked slab of cover between him
and all those blaster shots as he rushed into a flanking position.

The hitmen rushed to reposition, or maybe to get an angle.

A single deafening _/*BANG*/_ that popped his ears and damn near kicked
him in the ribs exploded out from the shops window behind him and to his
right, and he saw /someone – / along with the cover he’d been hiding
behind and whatever had been behind /them /– get completely pulverized
by whatever monster weapon Miss Militia was firing from inside the
building’s window.

The hitman exploded into gore, body parts, and bits of blood flying
everywhere. The assassin closest to the exploded corpse stumbled,
seemingly wondering what the hell happened before Dennis took the moment
to duck out of cover and land a shot on the man’s chest that knocked him
on his ass.

Not dead; their armor wasn’t cheap. But he was definitely hurting.

Dennis ducked back into cover. A second massive shot rang out from Miss
Militia’s perch; someone else died.

The hitmen were scrambling now, abandoning their thin cover of bone
benches and thin road signs for thicker support pillars and speeders.

He poked back out of cover, and was lining up a shot when someone
crashed into him from behind.

Dennis pitched forward. Old CQC training and experience in a handful of
brawls kicked in, letting him catch his fall and simultaneously twist in
his attacker’s grip.

His gun fell out of his hand, though, clattering across the floor as
Dennis landed on his back. His enemy was to his side, so the time-
stopping hero lashed out with his armored elbow, cracking it against a
helmeted and masked head.

He got two punches in the kidneys for his effort that sent bolts of
rolling agony through his entire side, robbing him of his strength as
his enemy drew a knife. It was pure reflex and instinct that had Dennis’
hand whip out to grab hold of the blade, the edge slicing his palm open
before he froze it in place.

“Wh-What the he-”

Taking advantage of the surprise, Dennis twisted on the floor, facing
his would-be assassin as he drew his holdout blaster and fired two shots
right into the man’s chest!

The two shots punched through the armor, and the Bando Gora hitman let
out a gasping shout, dying if not dead.

“There!”

Dennis’ eyes snapped up.Two more enemies with fully automatic rifles
were lining up their shots.

/Fuck!/

He jerked forward, both hands planting themselves on the dying hitman’s
chestplate before he yanked him close and twisted so his enemy was all
but draped over him.

Then he froze both the person and the armor.

The two other hitmen started firing, but the deluge of green blaster
fire failed to burn through their time-frozen friend, leaving Dennis
very much alive.

A third shot from Miss Militia’s gun rang out. With a third enemy dead
the rain of blaster fire let up, letting Dennis reach for his holdout
blaster. Firing two shots, he caught the remaining of that pair of
hitmen in the foot; he yelped and scrambled away.

Sirens started wailing, drawing closer.

There was a sharp, high-pitched whistle. Dennis dared to peek up, past
his dying cover, to where he saw the hitmen’s leader, and two others,
making tracks as fast as they could away from here.

Dennis sagged, relief flooding through him. It had been a while since
he’d been in a serious firefight like that.

A hand clamped down on his arm, and he damn near jumped out of his skin
before he recognized Militia’s face through his helmet visor.

“They’re after you!” she said. “Your ship!”

His brain stuttered for a moment, then realization hacked through his
fogged up brain.

“Rugess!” he scrambled to his feet, jumping over the still time-frozen
assassin, grabbing his main blaster off the floor and /sprinting/
towards the primary lift to get them back up to the hangar bays.

A security patrol speeder was fast approaching, its siren blaring
loudly, bright yellow lights flashing. It swerved, using the whole
speeder to cut them off before Dennis jumped onto the hood. As he
walked, stumbling, over the vehicle, he reached down, fingers brushing
the car roof.

The vehicle froze.

One door was half open, the passenger squawking in surprise as he
slammed his head into a windshield and door that wouldn’t budge. Other
shouts of alarm and surprise echoed out of the tiny opening in the door
as he and Militia ran as fast as they could away from the crime scene.

They wouldn’t be flying off Utapau any time soon.

Pushing a grocery cart.

Looking very confused and concerned.

“Why weren’t you answering your comms!”

Yeah. Didn’t make sense.

Still. Once burned, twice shy. And better overly cautious than overly dead

_/*Chapter 33:* / _

_/*Dooku:* / _

As Yan Dooku approached the hangar bay where the Vista was docked, A
warning shuddered through the Force, telling him that all was amiss, but
he wasn’t quite sure what.

The Force did not indicate violence would be needed; words would
suffice.Yet, he still kept his hand near the lightsaber at his side; it
would not do to be careless.

As he opened the hangar bay door, his eyes took in the sight of the /
Vista/ - a strange name for a ship with so poor a view from any window -
and saw it was utterly /wrecked/. So, that’s what the Force was alerting
him to.

He stepped into the hangar, and he realized too late that he had
misattributed the specifics of the warning when he felt the barrel of a
blaster against the back of his head.

“Alright, old man,” Kronos’ voice growled somewhere behind him, “we’re
gonna have an honest talk.” Dooku slowly raised his arms even as he
allowed the threads of the Force to reach and touch the young man’s hand
and fingers, ready to tighten their grip over his digits to keep him
from pulling the trigger. Difficult, but it was his only chance.

“I assure you, Kronos,” he said, only now catching sight of the rather /
large/ green rifle pointed straight at him from his right, held by the
Mandalorian woman, Hannah, who was laying down to increase her accuracy,
“I have been nothing but honest with you.”

“Yeah? Then why is it that after I stepped onto this planet, heading
towards your target, the next thing I know I’ve got a hit squad trying
to kill me. /Me,/ specifically. You’re the only one who could have told
them where the hell I was going.”

“Hmm. That is curious,” he said, mostly to himself, thinking aloud.

Kronos didn’t take it that way, misinterpreting his droll tone for a
taunt, pressing the barrel more firmly into the back of Dooku’s head.

“Don’t screw around, old man.”

Dooku shrugged carelessly, slowly lowering his hands to adjust his
sleeves. They had rolled up his arms while he had them raised. Unseemly.
“If I had arranged that ambush, and you had survived, I would not have
walked in here without my weapon drawn or without backup. What you’ve
said is new information to me.”

He turned around, staring down the barrel, making Kronos tense up.

Dooku laced his hands behind his back.

“/*Watch it,*” /the boy’s fingers tightened over the trigger.

Dooku was unphased, barely paying attention to the boy as he considered
things.

“Who was it that attacked you?” he asked. “The Hutts? Or another group?
Are you familiar with them? Do you have history?”

The boy’s grip on his weapon was white knuckled, his other fist clenched
just as tightly before the gun lowered ever so slightly

“Don’t know ‘em. Called themselves Bando Gora.”

Dooku stiffened. ”Ah.”

That name made things considerably more awkward.

The sound he released made the boy readjust his aim back to his head.
“You know something.”

“I do.” There was no point in obfuscating. “The Bando Gora are assassins
for hire. Their top leadership are usually Force-sensitive to a degree.”

“Like you?”

Dooku snorted. Ignorance. “/Not/ like me. Their leader, however… I know
her well. Her name is Komari Vosa. She wishes me dead. I’m afraid this
‘hit squad’ was after me, not you.”

“They didn’t mention you,” the boy pressed. “They called me out /by name./”

“You either have a contract set out against you, or Komari specifically
told them to-” he gestured between them. “Likely hoping /this/ would end
in one of our respective deaths. Either you kill me, or I kill you and
the others. Leaving me stranded and embroiled in a difficult position
with the local authorities.

A thought occurred to him then, and he glanced up and away from the boy.

“How long ago was the ship damaged?”

“Dunno,” Kronos mumbled. “An hour? Two? Taking that roundabout way
towards the smoke shop kept us for a while.”

“I take it Guriwik is dead as well?” he asked, still looking around the
hangar.

“Yeah,” Kronos shrugged, his gun still drawn but not pointed directly at
him. The Mandalorian woman, though, had not shifted her aim at all.
“Still doesn’t explain how the hell they’d know where we were headed.”

“That answer is simple,” Dooku commented, turning to walk away from the
now mollified boy. “The Sith knows I’m seeking information about Damask
and simply put a trap along the next breadcrumb.”

“Really putting the cart before the horse, there,” Kronos hissed, /
slowly/ holstering his blaster and signaling the Mandalorian to do the same.

“Do you have another explanation?” The question was rhetorical. Dooku
could /feel/ the confirmation in the Force; the Sith /knew/ what he was
doing.

He was getting /close/. This was all the confirmation he needed

He kept walking.

“Where the hell are you going?”

Dooku didn’t answer, rounding a corner. While he had taught Obi-Wan and
Anakin much, he’d learned a bit from them as well.

Namely, how one would ‘hack’ the security system of a highly monitored
hangar bay – perhaps to ‘borrow’ a ship that would be returned only
‘half crashed’, or in this instance, raid a freighter without any
authorities discovering the deed or interfering.

With a wave of his hand, two large cargo crates ground across the iron
floor with a screeching squeal.

“There,” he gestured.

A small slicer droid, disposable and preprogrammed, was still latching
itself onto the astromech port.

Kronos and the Mandalorian Woman both approached. The boy was still
cautious, still wary. The woman still had a weapon in hand, but it was a
far more reasonable size..

“How’d you know it was there?” Kronos asked accusingly.

Dooku rolled his eyes.

With a gesture he drew his saber, and with a snap hiss and a flick of
his wrist, the droid was in two pieces. He ignored both the Mandalorian
and the smuggler drawing their guns on him.

By the time he placed the hilt on his belt hook again, the alarms had
started blaring.

_/*Taylor:* / _

Halcyon was, thankfully, not like Coruscant.

Where Coruscant had buildings that were, effectively speaking, cities
unto themselves, with practically whole ecosystems living between their
walls and halls, Halcyon had cities that were more akin to those from
home. Individual buildings, streets, open spaces, and so on.

It helped. It really did. Sure, my powers in a Coruscant spire were
likely even more effective, given the sheer congestion, but it was /
harder/ to move ‘unnoticed’. After all, psychologically, you don’t
really notice someone crossing the street – you do, however, notice
someone walking down a hallway you were meant to guard.

But here, just the normal foot traffic of the city did more than enough
to conceal my and Windu’s movements.

We were dressed in civilian wear, of course. I was wearing a sort of
overgrown jacket that seemed to be in fashion here, and Master Windu was
in what I assumed to be normal work clothes, the equivalent of dress
pants and a button-up white shirt from back home.

He somehow seemed… /less/ without the robes. Less gravitas, less
powerful. Just… less.

It was definitely off-putting. But it was also good, because not
attracting attention was the goal.

We gave the guards and lookouts wide berth, drawing in close to the
building only where the lookouts had blindspots or when there was a
shift change. Windu hung back at times - like, a city block away - still
within my range and still able to reach me in seconds with a burst of
speed, if need be.

But there wasn’t a need. These guys were ready for Halcyon Security. An
eighteen-year-old girl didn’t even register on their radar.

Which was already actionable information, truth be told.

/“So, they are laying a trap for us?” /Minister Q’ou’s voice asked
through our earpiece.

“They are,” I nodded. “Can’t really tell what weapons they’ve got, but
they’re definitely rifles, not just hand blasters. I noted at least two
crates of explosives, and they have some heavy assault droids hidden
inside that building.”

“/Where in the void did they get assault droids?!”/

The question didn’t really seem directed at me, more a general ‘curse,’
so to speak. I shrugged, turning my gaze to Windu.

As we walked, the Jedi Master seemed deep in thought, his brow furrowed,
fingers cupping his chin.

I let him think, content to walk in silence.

As we rounded a corner, we reached an unmarked speeder. Close-topped, it
was the equivalent of a van with a sliding door back home. Though, if I
understood local vehicles correctly, this was a repurposed trash compactor.

The doors opened as we drew close, an agent gesturing for us to climb
in; we did, and the door shut behind us.

On the interior screens was a holo-layout of the building. It was a /
large/ place, a droid processor manufacturing plant. Or, at least, it
had been once. Most of that equipment seemed to have been ripped out
root and stem when the terrorists moved in, if not repurposed for other
ends.

The building’s surrounding grounds had two large courtyards at the north
and south ends, with the building itself splitting those areas off from
each other.

If I were any judge, they were once parking areas for the transport
trucks. Surrounding both those courtyards were high, angled walls, and
two stretched-out walkways for loading cargo. One high, one on ground
level. Made sense when you had flying cars.

Similarly, the building itself looked like a cross between a
manufacturing plant and a control tower in an airport. Again, made sense
when you had flying trucks to manage.

It had three levels: two “floors”, and a third that was the diamond-like
tower head itself.

Repurposed, as it was, with combat in mind, they had converted it into a
fortress with the walls and walkways altered to be ideal crossfire
locations. The building was now a glorified bunker, and the tower a
massive shooting platform and sniper’s nest.

My scouting with my insects had also revealed that they had well over
seventy people in there, ready to fight. The two droids I’d seen, I /
suspected/ were once heavy lifter droids – little more advanced than a
giant forklift, originally – but, mount a few guns on a toaster, and
it’ll start making more than just toast after a while…

…

Did it count as “fucking Tinkers” if it was /mundane/ tech here?

In short, anyone who marched in here had better be ready for a heavy
fight, or they were gonna have a very very bad day.

Windu took a seat in the truck’s passenger bay, arms crossed, still
thinking.

I sat down, too, listening to the chatter between Minister Q’ou, Master
Yaddle, and a few advisors on the other end of the line.

Finally, the Jedi Master opened his eyes. “Padawan Hebert, how would you
approach this problem?”

I’d been expecting the question, honestly. Windu, more than anyone
besides Yaddle, here, understood the extent of my powers and the level
of ‘omniscience’ I had.

I knew the layout of that place better than its builders after spending
most of the day with my bugs crawling all over it.

“Four pronged attack,” I answered simply, turning my head towards the
screen with the building on display. I noted that two of the three
agents in the back had ‘subtly’ turned their eyes and ears towards us.
‘Not listening.’

I got up, pointing at a drainage pipe I’d discovered towards the center
of the building’s foundation. “You and I come in from below. Maybe with
a squad, if you’d like to be cautious. We attack, cause a ruckus, and as
soon as the outer patrols start rushing in to help, attack from the two
courtyards with Master Yaddle. With /everyone/ distracted on ground
level, the last group comes in from above, through the tower. Hit them
fast, make it overwhelming and from all directions. They’ll fold.”

It was, after all, how I’d won most of the fights I’d had no right to win.

Windu’s eyes narrowed, frowning. “The first attack squad will be
engaging at a huge disadvantage. Low ground, surrounded, cut off from
reinforcements, with a difficult retreat route if things go wrong. And,
if they have sensors, or detect the squad approaching, things will be
even worse.”

“You’re not wrong,” I shrugged. “But, either way, you’ve got a fight on
your hands. Either take the gamble that lets you win as fast and clean
as possible, or you grind it out. There’s no way to get around it.”

“And negotiating their surrender?” He raised an eyebrow.

I…

… hadn’t considered that.

I almost reeled where I sat at the realization.

Why… /hadn’t/ I thought of that?

“You… /know/ they won’t accept that,” I said.

Again, a single eyebrow raised on the Master’s face.

“Don’t I?” he questioned. “The presence of a Jedi might sway them,” he
volunteered.

“And it might not. Then you throw away the element of surprise, causing
even more needless risk.” I wasn’t wrong, but it still bothered me: that
niggling… /something/ tickling the back of my thoughts that questioned
why I hadn’t even bothered considering talking.

I paused, mulling over anything else I could say.

“You labeled them terrorists,” I pressed.

“My opinions are immaterial to /your/ responses,” he dismissed, staring
at me intently. “A Jedi should always /consider/ peace, first and
foremost, as an option.” His stare told me he /knew/ I hadn’t. “Even if
they find they cannot take that option for whatever reason.”

I didn’t have much to say to that.

Silence fell over us.

“We will discuss our possible paths with Master Yaddle and Minister
Q’ou,” he finally concluded. “The Halcyon separatists will hold for a
few more hours until we decide on a course of action.”

I nodded.

_/*Hannah:* / _

“What I demand to understand is precisely what sort of backwards,

tripled, and an entirely new ship will be provided to yo-”

“You will /repair/ my vessel, Muun. I did not arrive in one of /your/
ships, I arrived on /mine,/ and I will be leaving with it.”

“O-of course, right away! I will send out the orders immediately.”

“See that you do.”

Hannah turned away from the exchange, casting her eyes towards the ship
itself. Rugess stood by the mangled entry ramp, wringing his hands
nervously as the various crime scene workers and police climbed in and
out, taking pictures and samples, and examining score marks and the
various points of damage.

Dennis paced, walking around in the relatively isolated area of the
hangar bay like a caged tiger, arms crossed, mask still firmly in place.

His worry and relief regarding Rugess had ebbed. His suspicions of the
Count had likewise receded, somewhat, leaving him with nothing but his
own mounting anger as he kept staring at his ship.

She heard rapid footsteps on the steel floors, the energy at her hip
whorling as though it would change for a moment, before she arrested the
urge and kept it as a knife.

Turning her head towards the sound of someone hastily approaching, she
saw one of the security officers rushing towards the Banking Clan
member, who was still doing his level best to keep his bowing head below
Dooku’s nose, allowing the older man to properly look down it.

The security officer handed the Banking Clan member a datapad. The Muun
looked at it briefly, then his eyes widened and snapped back to it as he
seized it to read it more thoroughly.

His face brightened, “This is excellent news, Master Dooku! One of the
suspects - a member of the group that attacked your employees in the
lower levels - he survived!”

“Oh?”

“Yes,” the Muun assured the Count, nodding with a pleased smile. “He
received two shots to the chest, but survived long enough for our medics
to arrive. We should be able to interrogate him once he regains
consciousness.”

“I would speak with this man,” the Count pressed. “He might respond to a
Jedi’s persuasion over more mundane means.”

“Ahhh… well… you see that is… somewhat irregular.”

“You will overlook the irregularity,” Dooku said, waving his hand in a
slow, seemingly dismissive gesture, “to make amends for this lapse in
security.”

“Of course,” the Muun answered dully, bowing again, his voice almost
resigned in how flat it was. “I will overlook this irregularity, to make
amends for this lapse in security.”

—--------------

By the time the security teams were packing up and leaving, the sun was
beginning to set. The sinkhole was now lit up by artificial lights
rather than sunlight, and the overhead skies were cast in brushstrokes
of orange fire and twilight purples.

The Count had wrangled out stays in a hotel along with added security
for the evening. Tomorrow they would go and ‘visit’ the survivor, and
see if they could wrangle some answers out of him.

“I trust I am cleared of suspicion.”

The old man’s voice was droll, losing none of that confident, well-worn
arrogance that pervaded his every act and mannerism.

Dennis still scratched the backside of his blaster’s handle with his
thumb, his fingernail grinding against the metal.

“I can’t think of a reason you’d try to make a backstab this elaborate,”
he finally admitted.

It was a fair assessment. To be frank, Hannah couldn’t fathom why
someone would try for something this elaborate either.

She would likely keep a close eye on the Count, but she had a feeling
that sentiment was more due to the close call, still fresh on their
minds and frayed nerves, than on any real basis.

Seeing how much sway the old man could bully the local security forces
into having his way, he could have had them both thrown in jail for a
very, very long time if he’d been behind this failed assassination attempt.

Dooku snorted through his nostrils. “Carry your suspicions on your own
time. Komari Vosa has stranded us on this planet for a reason; likely
this first attack was merely an exploratory one. An attempt to draw me
out, or leave me isolated here.”

Hannah crossed her arms. “So, what’s her next move?” she ventured to
ask. “You know her better than us.”

“The young woman I knew would have wished for a confrontation,” he
answered. “Tomorrow, we will go to see her assassin, but in truth, I
suspect we won’t /truly/ need his information. She will seek me out,
instead.” A fond smile graced his features. “My students would say
something inane, to simply walk forward and /spring the trap/ as it were.”

“You disagree, I hope?” she asked; that sounded like a supremely ill-
advised idea.

Dooku shrugged. “I’ve… repurposed their methods,” he answered carefully.

_/*Taylor:* / _

My plan was adopted.

Mostly.

The general idea still held, but neither Windu nor Yaddle were at all
comfortable in placing me in the first ‘wave’, even though that’s where
I felt I could do the most good. Neither of them wanted to order a
Padawan into the ‘teeth’ of the fighting.

Windu would be taking my place, and a squad of, well, /SWAT/ – or at
least this planet’s equivalent in the security force – would be at his back.

Heavy weapons, body armor, the works.

Yaddle would lead the attack on the north side courtyard.

I would be entering from above with the last attack wave, the one that
should receive the least amount of resistance.

I understood the precaution. I got /why/ they felt like they had to
protect me, but it was a waste. That initial squad could remain hidden
with me in their team, and get into a position to cause /huge/ damage if
I were guiding them.

Maybe Windu could do the same by following the vague, nebulous warnings
of the Force – he was a Master, after all – but “vague and nebulous”
wasn’t the cold, hard certainty of insect-based tracking and local
omniscience.

I chafed under the decision, but I knew better than to protest. Both
Windu and Yaddle were… protective personalities. If it were Yoda – who
enjoyed experimenting – or perhaps Master Plo – who trusted me to know
my capabilities – I might be able to convince them. But not these two.
Not for this.

Minister Q’ou wanted to get started immediately, so as not to give the
rebels the chance to catch wind or make any changes to their defenses. I
also understood /that/ sentiment as well. He apologized for the rush,
recognizing we’d scarcely had a chance to rest before being thrust into
this.

But for all his apologies, he still implored us to help regardless.

It took several hours to organize a raid of this size.

Which… fair enough. It was gonna be a /big/ raid.

Three gunships. Six armored vehicles. Twenty squads (around a hundred
and twenty men). A force like this would have been assembled to back up
the Protectorate if they were going to seriously strike at Lung or
Kaiser back home. So, Minister Q’ou wasn’t exactly tossing a hasty,
understrength force at this problem and hoping the sleep-deprived Jedi
would just carry it to a win.

And, to be even more fair, the minister wasn’t exactly caught up on
sleep, either, as far as I could tell.

So we were dismissed while the preparations were underway, which gave
Windu, Yaddle and me some precious hours to catch some of that coveted
sleep.

By the time we woke up some three hours later, the sun had /long/ since
set. It was approaching the galactic standard hour of 19:20, but, for
this part of this planet, that was closer to an equivalent to three or
four am.

In short, those separatists were probably tired and sleeping as well.

Even better.

I sat in the gunship with the squad of troopers, waiting. The engines
were spooled up and ready to launch, but still… waiting. Waiting for
Master Windu. Waiting for Master Yaddle. Waiting for command to give the
order to scramble out.

The weight in my hand was heavy. Not my lightsaber.

We were four minutes away at top speed. Which was mind-boggling to me.
We weren’t anywhere close to that separatist base. At a /guess,/ it was
the equivalent of the distance between Boston and New York. /Four
minutes/ made it feel like we were just a stone’s throw away.

I listened to comms. Mace didn’t have my level of awareness, but he had
experience. He was careful, cautious. More than once, he’d avoided a
patrol as far as I could tell. He let his techs scan for traps and
sensors as they progressed. He was in no rush, showed no anxiety. This
was a job, one he’d done countless times before.

The squadron with me was a different matter.

I could sense their nervousness, their anxiety. It suffused and
suffocated the inside of the gunship. It was easy to block out, but
still annoying. Distantly, I could sense Master Yaddle’s Force
signature. As ever, the small woman was sending eddies of calming Force
energy to those around her, easing anxious hearts and steeling resolve.

I wondered, for a brief moment, how much good that ability – that /
woman/ – could do back on Earth. Against things like the Slaughterhouse
Nine, or the Endbringers. And then felt a pang of guilt at the thought
of placing her against those monsters. And then I strangled a knife of
fear and panic in its proverbial cradle before it could overwhelm me.

Those memories weren’t mine. They. W/eren’t/. Mine.

The weight in my hand felt like lead.

I heard the sharp chirp of a blaster go off on my comms.

A brief, half second of silence.

Then another, and a third.

A crackling hiss.

_/*“This is Jedi Master Windu with the first strike team. Contact
established with insurgents! Second and third waves, begin your
attack!”* / _

I heard the sound of rifles being primed, weapons checked, and the
engines beginning to howl.

But all those sounds were quiet, muffled things, compared to the buzzing
of insects in my mind.

_/*Gavorn:* / _

 

It was textbook.

Halcyon security had one way of doing things.

Slow and loud.

Be it their public relations, their police work, or anything else.
Everything they did was slow and loud.

They’d hired back that fossil, Q’ou, from the fucking graveyard he was
stuffed into. But the old relic wouldn’t change things. Certainly not
enough to run the security forces with any form of competence.

When they came for them, they were supposed to literally /see/ them
coming. Walk right into the teeth of their guns under a hail of blaster
fire. They would give them a bloody nose, then slip out. The few boys
that got captured could be busted out when they were transported to New
Koren prison.

Then the bastards came up from below.

Worse than that, they showed up with a /Jedi/.

No one was supposed to know about that tunnel. He’d checked that
himself. It had been purged from all the official plans and blueprints
of the whole sector. It would carry them to tunnel 4-F on the east side,
an abandoned maglev cavity, and they’d simply walk right out. By the
time Halcyon security knew where the kark they’d escaped through, they’d
be long bloody gone.

Instead, the karking bastards had hauled themselves up through that same
freakin’ tunnel.

Even so, he figured they could have held that line. They /should/ have
held that line. Eight men and one Jedi. Down in the lower pits, it was a
shooting gallery. Or, it should have been.

Then, the catwalks and railings had just… fallen down. Chains broke,
railings bent, and whole sections ripped themselves from their moorings,
making his boys plummet down to the ground. The Jedi had jumped /–
jumped – /damn near thirty feet to get at them, swinging that purple
blade. He cut off Larn’s hand and punched Korelli so hard, Gavorn was
pretty damn sure the bastard’s chest caved in. Korelli was a Whiphid!
How do you cave in one of /their/ chests with your bare hands?!

Then he heard other calls on the radio. Front and south courtyards. The
auto-defenses came up, blastin’ away, but without organic hands and
minds to do the actual fightin’, the auto-defenses were shit. And there
was another Jedi, a tiny green thing, hoppin’ around, bouncin’
everywhere and causin’ more mayhem.

The karkin garden gnome had ripped their heavy duty droids off the
ground without even touchin’ ‘em, slamming them through walls like a
wrecking machine, tearing ‘em apart and rippin’ flankin’ routes open so
the damn security teams could lay into the boys any time they tried to
form any kind of resistance.

He didn’t know how in the blue Corellian hell he made it out of that
mess, but before he knew it, just him and the twenty or so men that were
left were scramblin’ up the tower. If he was fast enough, he could get
to one of the jetpacks they had stashed there; they didn’t have a lot of
fuel, but they sure as shit had enough to get him out of this bloody mess!

He peered down, over the edge of the stairs. There was still a mess of
red and green blaster fire being exchanged, and the purple and green
blades of those Jedi were still visible through the smoke. Men screamed,
droids sparked. Fires began to turn the world beneath him orange. The
smoke stung his eyes and throat.

He climbed the stairs faster.

The world below was wreathed in flame, the world above midnight black.

He heard a sound: a buzzing, a loud droning in his ears, and he wondered
what in the Sith hell it was, even as he kept running.

One of the boys made it to the tower’s door ahead of him. Gavorn was
already out of breath even as the man pawed at the access codes.

Gavorn coughed, smoke making to the back of his throat while the man
fumbled with the controls. After a few tries, the man finally opened the
blasted door!

He shoved his way to the front, damn near throwing bastards to the floor
as he forced his way through the door.

The air up here was still crisp and clean, the smoke hadn’t gotten
through all the vents yet. He sucked down a deep, grateful breath of air.

The lights flickered on, illuminating the darkened room filled with
deactivated consoles and stockpiled weapons, including long rifles and
disruptor torpedo launchers.

And there, towards the very back, jetpacks, twelve of them. Enough to
field a jump pack squadron. He started moving, rushing forward quickly
to snag one, his hand gripping his blaster in case one of these karkin’
bastards learned to do some goddamn math in the next few minutes and
realized there weren’t enough to go around.

As he rushed forward, midstep, a shaft of /light,/ bright and white, cut
into his eyes, making him wince with the blinding radiance.

He almost put it out of his mind, almost kept running. He could hear the
others behind him, too damn many just as focused on the jetpacks as he was.

He looked around, a slow, creeping realization dawning on him.

The others didn’t notice. Too stupid. Too blind. Eighteen men scrambled
for whatever gear they could find… and they didn’t notice a karkin’ thing.

They were in the tower. The tower with window panes. The tower that
could be used to see across half the fuckin city in any direction.

And yet the windows were pitch black.

He stared at the glass, trying to see what was blocking their view. They
weren’t like those fancy panes that could become a two-way mirror
depending on the current put through them. The city never turned off its
lights.

He squinted…

He stared, blinking, leaning closer. Because he must be seeing wrong…

The windows couldn’t be covered frame to frame in writhing, /skittering/
bugs.

He breathed heavily.

Where the warm air from his lungs fogged the pane, a thunderous, bone-
rattling /*CRACK*/ sent a snaking fissure straight through it.

In the next instant – before he could scream – the glass /shattered/.

He’d remember that moment until his dying day.

It wasn’t the bugs crawlin’ over his face. It wasn’t the scream from the
boys. It wasn’t the all encompassing /darkness/ that swallowed his whole
world, or even the terror that came /later/.

It was the noise.

The droning, hissing, /buzzing/ /*noise.*/

A noise that vibrated through your whole body, from your head to your
toes, that shook the air in your lungs and made the bones in your body
feel like they’d vibrate off your muscles.

A noise so deep you’d /drown/ in it.

The men screamed. Blaster shots rang out, arms wielding them flailing.
He heard the door slam shut like an iron gate, sealing, even as someone
tried pounding away at it, desperate to escape.

He wasn’t sure how many she got before he finally saw her.

The yellow blade came first. Bright, shining. It cut weapons in two,
fists and bone breaking force taking men down after.

Then it disappeared.

He’d see it again a second later, far away, too far away. That time, an
arm was cut, not a gun. He barely caught the faintest hint of a
silhouette through the gloom before the blade vanished again.

It appeared closer when he saw it next. Too close. He heard the man
choking, a dark hand, its grip like iron, wrapped around his throat. His
fingers were clawing at the forearm that held him up as he tried to
struggle free.

That’s when he saw /her/: the nightmare

Eyes of yellow gold, too large for her face. Tendrils of ink for hair, a
hissing mouth of too many teeth, and a face of gray flesh.

He wasn’t the only one.

Another one of the boys, one of the last, aimed for her, rifle firing
from the hip. That particular karker knew we didn’t have a lot of time
before she disappeared again.

Something moved through the dark. A mass. It was only when it came into
the faint edges of the yellow light that he saw it was one of the
derelict consoles.

The shots hit the steel, tearing through metal and burnt wiring before
it was sent hurtling through the blackness and buzzing bodies.

Gavorn doubted the idiot ever saw the train that hit him.

Gavorn finally settled his own rifle, ready to pull the trigger.

He felt a grip at his throat, sudden and unyielding, cutting off the air
from his lungs. His chest hitched, his grip on his weapon losing all
strength, falling from his hands in the sudden blind panic of not being
able to breathe.

He moved to kneel down to grab the rifle again, and shoot her before he
was choked to death.

Then he was lifted off his feet, body going straight as he was pulled
across the room, boots scraping against the floor before he fell into
the grip that felt like it was ready to tear open his throat with bare
fingers.

The edges of his vision were growing dark, the utter and complete
blockage of his windpipe rapidly sapping him of whatever strength he
might still have.

The yellow blade drew closer, and he could see the nightmare looming
over him in her full, terrifying form.

She didn’t say a word.

When the world went dark, he wasn’t sure if it was his lack of
breathing, or the bugs that had devoured all the light in the world.

All he knew was that the sound – that horrid, overpowering noise – faded
away into an equally drowning _/*silence*/_.

_/*Yaddle* / _

Master Yaddle, more than most on the Council, often felt that the Force…
whispered to her.

A touch on her cheek. A breeze across her ear. Small nudges here and
there, that if one only /listened, stopped/ and allowed themselves to /
hear,/ they could follow.

It was hard, to be sure. Only Qui-Gon, dear boy, could seemingly grasp
it as readily as her. Or, perhaps, could remove himself enough to do so.

Perhaps that’s why Dooku had reached out to be her friend. A way to
better understand his beloved student.

Right here and now, amidst the noise, and the pain, the many calls for
all kinds of attention all competing with each other… In the aftermath
of the attack, it was difficult.

But still, she tried.

Because she felt, just as strongly, that it was important.

And so she listened.

She walked away from the pain, the distractions. She left Master Windu
to oversee it. The boy would do a good job, she knew that.

Her steps carried her upwards. Past the medics, past the police and
investigators still moving about the area. Past the prisoners, shackled
by the railings.

Up up. Higher.

Nudge her, the Force did. Until she could feel it.

Tightly wound. So /tight/ it hurt. Like a muscle tensed to the point of
tearing, and yet held there still, the pain ever increasing but the
consequence of releasing it so much /more/ painful.
Her small, clawed hand waved; the door opened at her urging through the
Force.

And there she was.

She stood on the walkways overlooking the courtyard. Sitting down on the
grated floors, knees held up to her chest, dark hair forming an inky
curtain.

In her hands… a mask.

Chitinous. Insect like. Its yellow eyes gleaming in the sunlight.

Her grip over its edges was tight. So tight it must have hurt. And yet
she dared not let it go.

“It's done,” the poor child whispered.

Yaddle stepped closer.

The tempest raged again, the winds howled. Jagged rock and crashing waves.

Yaddle’s heart /bled/.

/Oh… Padawan./

“This is what I had to do, right?” she asked, fingers kneading the edges
of this /thing/ in her hands. “I did it, then.”

Yaddle didn’t answer. Instead, she stepped closer to the poor girl.

The youngling lurched forward, shoving the mask at her and Yaddle took
it from her hands, divesting her of its physical presence, but not of
the gyre of sheer /horror /still surrounding her heart.

The poor girl shuddered.

Carefully, quietly, Yaddle set the mask down, its yellow eyes staring
sightlessly towards the sky.

Then, she closed the remaining distance, tiny arms reaching up, to pull
the girl close, and hold her tightly.

It was, perhaps, awkward. She was so much smaller that the girl’s head
was all she could hold properly, but Hebert merely /shuddered/. Her
whole body released a single horrid shake as desperate breaths shook
free of her lungs.

Her arms wrapped around Yaddle, clutching tightly as the old Master
rubbed a claw through her hair.

/“Taylor… it's- I’mTaylor. M-My name is T-”/

Her voice shook, then cracked, and finally broke. Mewling in her tears
and breathless sobs as Yaddle rocked this girl – her Padawan – as gently
as she could.

_/*Chapter 34:

Vicky:*/_

Zygerria really was a beautiful place, unlike any she’d seen before.

It reminded her of ancient depictions of Persia or the Middle East. The
architecture was an eclectic mix of Mayan and ancient Egyptian, in a sense.

Add to that the cat people and… well… it was almost like a theme park or
something.

Honestly, the stealth factor was just adding to the mystique of the
whole thing.

And she /was/ being stealthy. Yoda would vouch for her.

She floated above the city streets, watching the comings and goings of
the people, particularly from the palace. If she was gonna catch
something suspicious, it’d be there.

She heard a quiet sigh from her shoulder. Curious, she turned her head,
finding a strange expression on Yoda’s face as he stared down into the city.

“Something up?” she asked, her eyebrow hiking up to rest somewhere near
her forehead.

“Memory. Long, it is,” the little gremlin sighed, pointing with his
stick towards a building that dominated the skyline, just in front of
the palace. “A command center, it was.” The stick shifted to the market
square. “A final stand. General Kordac. Fierce, the fighting was.”

Vicky’s brain stuttered for a moment, mind desperately trying to catch
up before things clicked.

“You were here,” she whispered, realization in her voice. “You were one
of the Jedi that came with the Republic and brought down the Zygerrian
slave empire six hundred years ago.”

Yoda nodded, eyes distant and cloudy with memory.

She so very often forgot that Yoda was more than just everyone’s lovable
grandpa with a stick and a listening ear. He was a relic who’d lived and
breathed /hundreds/ of years of history. A living, breathing witness to
countless events.

“What was it like?” she ventured to ask, the wind catching her voice.
“Fighting back then? Seeing the differences now? Is it weird or… are
you, like, used to it?”

“Always strange, it is. But good as well,” he nodded. “Seeing the
passage of time, the changes to the galaxy, its people.”

“But not all change is good,” she argued. “In fact, I’ve read the
records.” She and Tay both had, in an effort to catch up with galactic
history they’d spent /months/ at a time doing nothing but reading books
and dataslates, especially regarding the Jedi and the Republic. “The
Jedi were… I don’t know. Stronger? Better?”

Now, Yoda turned his head, looking at her. “As strong as needed, the
Jedi Order is?”

“/Are/ you!?” she couldn’t keep the incredulity from her voice. “The
Republic had an army back then. One that could /stop/ slavery like this,
and /did/. Now it doesn’t even have that, and the Jedi Order is smaller
and weaker than ever-Ow.”

The complaint was more reflex than anything. The light boop on her
forehead was hardly anything more than the little green man looking to
interject, she knew the difference.

“Fighting is not the Jedi way. Strength measured it should not be-”

“But it shouldn’t be /discarded,/ either,” she contested, arms crossed.
“You guys are supposed to be peacekeepers but, frankly, you don’t have
the /numbers/ for peacekeeping. The Jedi Order numbered nearly half a
million by the time of the Ruusan Reformations, and now you’re barely
cracking ten thousand. And how many of /those/ are Padawans? If you guys
placed just ONE Jedi on ONE planet, you wouldn’t even cover the
primary /core/ worlds, let alone the rest of the galaxy that /actually/
needs help! It just…” she sighed.

“Passionate about this subject, you are,” Yoda observed, not unkindly.

She took a moment to gather her thoughts. Trying to find a way to word…
everything.

“I just feel like…” she sighed again. “I feel like you guys just… take
it for /granted/ that everything will be ok. That things /can’t/ get
‘bad’. But me and… and especially Tay. We’ve /seen/ how bad things get
when there simply aren’t enough /good/ people to put out every fire. And
from everything I’ve seen and read, the Jedi have been sliding /into/
that exact scenario,” she said. “You guys just… you’ve had things ‘under
control’ for so long you’re not seeing that the status quo of things
being peaceful and good only lasts as long as it's maintained. Cared for
like a garden. If you don’t have enough gardeners…” she trailed off

“Hmmm,” Yoda rubbed at his chin. Not agreeing. But not disagreeing
either. “What solution would you offer?”

“Start expanding again?” she answered instantly. “Hell, if you need help
convincing the others, I’m sure me and Tay can give you guys charts.
Half a million to ten thousand is a /drop/-” she started, a thought
occurring to her. “You must remember what it was, and how it changed. It
must’ve happened bit by bit but when you look at the two extremes… well…”

Yoda’s features fell, suddenly looking every single one of his years.
She felt… a little bad at making him feel whatever he was feeling, but
this had been something that /needed/ to be said. She really did feel
like the Jedi were reaching a crisis point in terms of how little they
could actually help the galaxy.

/Ten thousand/ to cover a /galaxy/ was /laughably/ small. Gross
negligence was a word that very well could apply.

A feeling tickled the back of her mind, a fluttering whisper of excited
anticipation.

She turned her head, following the feeling in the Force and from the
Fragile One to see someone with a pair of palace guards marching, very
determinedly towards… well… something.

She pointed. “Wanna check that guy out?”

“Hrm,” Yoda nodded. “Trust in your feelings, you should.”

“Ok then,” she chirped, slowly descending from the skies above. “My
feelings say, ‘screw that guy in particular’, so let’s go!

Yoda chuckled.

_/*Dooku:*/_

The Utapau security complex, like all of their structures, was a tight,
claustrophobic space; its hallways narrow, its ceilings low. The support
columns of thick white bone gave every structure the feeling of walking
through the bowels of some monstrous, long dead beast.

Kronos was not accompanying him at the moment, too busy overseeing the
promised repairs to the Vista alongside the Bith, Rugess. Instead, the
Mandalorian woman shadowed his steps. If his memory served, she had some
experience in law enforcement, so perhaps she would be useful in this
venture.

The officer escorting them was a Pau’an – long limbs, gaunt face, grey
flesh. Regardless, he bowed low as he addressed them, no doubt
instructed to show obeisance by the banking representatives in control
of this system.

“This is all of the evidence our officers have discovered since the
investigation began,” the alien said, handing Dooku a /single/ datapad.

The Count began to browse the security teams’ findings.

The assassins fled towards Sector 15-G. Said sector was cordoned off at
the moment, and was being actively searched as well. Their armor had
been permitted through checkpoints, but their weapons had been smuggled
through; illegal mods had made them invisible to scanners.

They’d arrived just sixteen hours ahead of Dooku’s own party. They had
killed the Rodian, Guriwik, approximately four hours later, so he had
been dead twelve hours before Dooku’s own arrival.

They had reached the hangar bay by taking transport terminal nine,
originating from the fourth floor, Subsector D, where they’d apparently
been staying in a local hotel: The Caliphaten.

The four rooms had been paid for in advance, for a week, in cash.

That information was useful. It told him the Sith didn’t know /exactly/
where Dooku was. He merely had /guesswork/ on that front. Otherwise, why
spend needless money on getting your squad of assassins a place to stay
for a week when they’d only realistically use it for less than a day.

The Mandalorian woman stood at his shoulder, reading over it.

How inconsiderate of him.

He looked to the Pau’an officer, glaring down his nose at the man. “A
copy, if you please.” It was not a request. “So my associate might read
the reports as well.”

The officer looked startled, then winced in apparent shame before
hastily bowing and rushing to go make a copy.

He drifted his eyes down to keep reading.

The assassins’ weaponry was illegally modified, though that was
unsurprising. Even beyond the scrambling tech that made them invisible
to scanners, there was evidence on the weapons fire impacts along the
walls and the Rodians body that showed significantly higher discharge
outputs than normal. Something he would need to keep in mind if he found
himself deflecting their blasters in the near future. The impact on his
saber would be significantly greater than a standard shot.

Preliminary examination of the corpses – and, of course, the live
prisoner – showed that the Bando Gora were also under the influence of
narcotics.

Several. Including multiple illegal combat stims. Something else he
could use. Addicts were weak-minded, after all.

The officer returned, bowing once again as he handed the Mandalorian
woman her own dataslate. She nodded, offering a shallow bow of her own
in thanks as she took it and began reading for herself.

Hmmm… Surveillance footage had detected approximately sixteen members of
the Bando Gora – or at least sixteen people participating in this
mission – but no sign of Komari on any of their instruments. No doubt,
her absence was to avoid this exact scenario.

“That’s odd.”

Slightly startled at the woman’s voice, Dooku turned, raising an
eyebrow. “What is?”

The woman scrolled up and down the datapad as if searching for
something, her eyes narrowing.

“Their arrival,” she answered. “The reports tell us when they arrived,
but not through what transport. Or what hangar bay.”

He scrolled back up to the arrival times and noted that she was, indeed,
right. It wasn’t listed. He hadn’t noticed because it would otherwise be
immaterial, but the utter lack of record immediately made it suspect.

“Officer,” he called, making the Pau’an straighten where he stood. “The
records regarding the transport vessel used by the assassins, where are
they?”

He handed the alien his datapad, watching as the officer’s expression
became strained before he handed it back.

“I’m sorry sir, if the information is not present it either hasn’t been
found or has been redacted due to security reasons.”

“Redacted,” he growled somewhere in his throat. Because if they got the
time and the hangar bay they arrived in, then it couldn’t be the
alternative. “On whose authority!?”

The Pau’an officer cringed away from Dooku, inching back and holding his
hands up in a warding gesture. “I’m afraid I cannot say, sir.”

Dooku’s irritation spiked. A flash of annoyance cutting through his calm.

This inquiry was certainly not over, but for now…

“Where is the prisoner?”

“Thraus Hospital, sir,” the officer answered. “I’ve been told you’d like
to speak with him; an escort is prepared to lead you there whenever
you’re ready.”

“Then we will go /now/.”

_/*Vicky*/_

You know… for a galaxy with flying cars, people looked up remarkably
little; just like home.

… Actually, come to think of it: Would having flying cars sensitize or
desensitize people to looking up? At home, if you saw something in the
air out of the corner of your eye, you’d probably look up. Here, maybe not…

Huh…

Questions for later.

As she floated above the… whoever he was, Vicky drifted just close
enough to listen as he spoke on holo to multiple people. He treated each
with varying degrees of either politeness or disdain, but nothing
incriminating, at least not yet.

Then, finally he hung up with the latest conversation and-

“I take it you’ve heard, the Republic sent Jedi-”

She tossed Yoda a look, and the little green goblin remained clinging at
her shoulder, eyes closed but his ears perked all the way up to try and
listen in better.

“-Right. They’re confined to the palace for now. That gives us time to
move the shipment somewhere more secure.”

Bingo.

She tensed, ready to swoop down, pluck the little bastard up by his
hairs if need be and fly /up/ until they were breathing clouds. People
tended to get /talkative/ when they were at a point where they could hit
terminal velocity.

But before she could do much more than start the motion to dive down,
Yoda’s hand tapped her on the shoulder, shaking his head; telling her no.

/“Why?”/ she whispered.

“Seen, we must not be,” Yoda reminded her. “Master Gallia’s task,
difficult enough it is. The laws, we must obey.”

She opened her mouth, then shut it, crossing her arms with a huff of air
as she kept floating above the slaving bastard to keep listening.

“How long can they be held there?”

There was a pause as the answer came through, but it was impossible to
hear through the man’s earpiece.

“Good. The Jedi should be gone within that time once they find nothing.
They’ve requested the financial records of the entire court. I’ll be
sure to keep your name out of it. No. They won’t find anything wrong
with mine, I assure you.”

Vicky grinned.

Perfect.

They didn’t have a name, but she was sure they could narrow down the
list of suspects with what she already knew.

Yoda evidently agreed. With another tap against her shoulder, he
signaled her to retreat. She gently drifted away until the man and his
guards were out of earshot.

“Return to Master Gallia, we should,” Yoda said. “Our time, almost up it
is.”

She nodded. Honestly, she hadn’t really been paying attention to their
allotted curfew of an hour and fifteen minutes, but she supposed it /
was/ getting close to that time.

Approaching their rooms from the air, Vicky aimed for the open large-
frame window that led to the common area of their residential wing,
perfectly timing her entrance with the curfew set by Adi Gallia. "Tah-
dah!" she proclaimed, smiling as she touched down with hands stretched
out to take a showman's bow. "See? No harm done, and we found out
something very interesting!"

Adi had been pacing at the center of the room, hands behind her back. At
Vicky's entrance, she sighed, her shoulders sagging with unmistakable
relief.

“Oh, thank the Force,” she breathed. “Go and get changed, we can discu-”

There was a knock at their door.

/“Masters Jedi, we’ve been tasked with inspecting your rooms-”/

The door began to open.

Yoda /immediately/ jumped up, off her shoulder and onto the chandelier.
Vicky, startled, wondered if this was some kind of pavlovian response of
his because /that/ reaction sure as shit wasn’t normal!

Then she realized what /she/ looked like. Dressed in what was
certainly /not/ sleep wear or anything you’d wear if you were staying in
your room, her hair and clothes sprinkled with sand.

She definitely couldn’t be seen like this.

Adi damn near shoved her towards her room, but the door started to open
before she got there.

So Vicky did the only thing she could think of.

She floated up, onto the high ceiling, hiding just above the entry door.

Adi’s face of pure /stricken/ panic was… absolutely hilarious.

And in the next instant it was gone, replaced with placid calm that
would have given Tay a run for her money on the poker face nationals as
three guards entered the common area.

“Guardsmen,” she drawled, “how may I help you?”

The lead guardsman bowed. “Lady Jedi, forgive the intrusion. But we’ve
heard some reports that require us to inspect your rooms and make
certain you’re complying with the royal edict to remain here until
you’re cleared.”

“This is /most/ insulting, guardsman,” Adi sneered, straightening as she
clasped her hands behind her back, drawing herself up to her full
height. “We are Jedi, and we obey the laws of the Republic and sovereign
planets we visit.”

“I understand, ma’am. Just following orders,” the guardsman gestured
towards the rooms.

Vicky glanced up from the back of the guards towards the chandelier-

Yoda was gone.

She stared at the spot where the little green man should be, only to
confirm that, yes – the little green gremlin was /missing/ from the
chandelier. The glass chandelier that should have tinkled and made
plenty of noise when he moved…

Like… impressive… but also… How?

One guardsman entered her room, the other Yoda’s.

Not five seconds later, Yoda’s guard exited; regretting his life choices
as a stick was clanging rather loudly against his armored shins.

*_/*Clang*/_* “Most rude, this is!” *_/*Clang*/_* “Intrusive, it is!”
*_/*Clang*/_!*

“Ow! Sir! Please! I didn’t mean to interrupt your nap!”

*_/*CLANG*/_* “Meditating, I was!”

Her guardsman exited her room. “Sir, I can’t find the third one.”

“She’s in the refresher,” Adi answered immediately.

The guard captain nodded. “We’ll wait to confirm-”

“Guardsman,” Adi’s voice dropped an octave, pure /anger/ in her tone.
“You will not /wait/ for my Padawan to exit the refresher in a state of
undress so you might /inspect/ for yourself. You have your confirmation.
Get. Out.”

The man paused, and for a moment Vicky wondered if he’d call Adi’s bluff.

Then he sighed, gesturing to his two men.

“We’re done. Let’s go,” he turned back towards Adi Gallia, nodding.
“Sorry for the intrusion, ma’am. Thank you for your cooperation.”

_/**Clang**/_

“Ow!” The guard hobbled rather quickly out of Yoda’s reach, muttering
about how his armor was useless.

As the door shut behind the three guardsmen, Adi’s entire mask crumpled,
revealing the thousand yard stare of a woman that had just looked at bad
potential futures in the face and didn’t appreciate the experience.

Vicky sloooooowly floated towards her door. “I’mma go… take a shower
now… yeah…”

She shut the door before Adi could gather herself for the full reprimand
she just /knew/ was coming.

A shower sounded really, /really/ good right about now, actually.

…

Maybe a long soak.

_/*Dooku:*/_

The medical room held the sharp, stinging scent of antiseptics,
disinfectants and chemical cleaning supplies. The monitoring equipment
beeped and blooped with the rhythmic tracking of the prisoner’s vitals.

The prisoner himself was conscious – his surface thoughts were obvious
enough for that – though his eyes were closed. A tube was stuffed down
his throat, his limbs shackled to the railings of his hospital bed, and
bandages slathered with bacta were draped over his chest where,
apparently, Kronos had shot him twice. It was a small miracle he’d survived.

Quietly, Dooku stepped inside the room. The hiss of the door made the
prisoner’s eyes open, and the immediate hostility and recognition was a
most welcome thing. It would keep things from dragging on for too long.

The Mandalorian woman stepped in behind him, and as she did, Dooku
sensed the man’s sharp spike of fear.

Interesting.

Floating a chair over to set it beside the bed, Dooku sat in the cheap
furniture as if enthroning himself. “You know who I am.” It wasn’t a
question. “As such, I know who it is that assigned you this task. I’d
prefer to make things quick. Where is she?”

Dooku slid a pad and pen towards the man, slipping the writing utensil
into his grip. The assassin glanced at the tool, then back to Dooku, no
doubt contemplating if he could use it to finish the job.

“Don’t try it,” he warned.

The assassin’s eyes narrowed, but then he shrugged, though the movement
caused him to wince in sudden, unexpected pain.

He began to write.

Dooku waited for a moment, letting the man scratch at the pad with the
point of the pen before he stopped.

Pulling the pad free he read the words.

_/*“Vosa wants you to know. Only reason I’m saying anything. She won’t
stay on Utapau. If you want to face her, you’ll leave the system and
face her. Alone.”*/_

That explains why she targeted the ship. She wished him isolated. A
trap, no doubt.

“Where?” he asked, once again sliding the pad under the man’s hand.

The man scribbled down his answer.

_/*“Mining platform 13611 - Outer Rim. Galvatros system.”*/_

Hmmm. Galvatros system. Quite a distance from here. Remote. There would
be few, if any people passing through.

It was also far away from any known Bando Gora holdings.

Another reason to target the ship. To delay his leaving. Give her time
to ‘set the stage’, as it were.

He would be walking into a trap. “I see,” he drawled. “Thank you.”

He pulled the pad and the pen free. The Mandalorian woman tossed him a
questioning look. He shook his head. “Not here”

She followed him out the door with nary a complaint as the cogs in
Dooku’s mind began to turn.

He was not like his two foolish students. He would not simply go and
“spring the trap”.

He was not above using it for himself, however.

_/*Yarael Poof*/_

Yarael Poof wasn’t used to being in command of the Jedi Council.

To be frank, it was rare for both Master Yoda and Master Windu to be out
on missions simultaneously, and therefore rare for another member to be
assigned as head of the Council in their absence.

But, it had happened now for Padawan Dallon and Hebert’s Jedi Trials,
and so, the task had fallen to him this time.

He’d hoped things would stay relatively quiet but, alas, that was not
the case. Particularly today, when they’d received this message from, of
all people, Siri Tachi.

“What should be done?” he asked his fellow Council members

Saesee Tiin rubbed at his jaw, glowering at the holo message. “Padawan
Tachi has never once asked us for any kind of assistance. If she’s
asking now, I’m inclined to provide it.”

“As am I,” Plo-Koon added. “I see no reason why we should not send aid
immediately. The Bando Gora are a known assassin guild, one that
actively seeks out and indoctrinates Force-sensitives. If not us, then
who is to contend with them?”

“Whilst I understand the concern,” Master Koth cut in, “should we not
also be concerned about Padawan Tachi? Acting on this information might
reveal her as a spy if it’s traced back to her.”

“Our success is not guaranteed, either,” Master Rancisis pointed out,
serpentine body rippling as he moved in his seat. “The Jedi contended
with the Bando Gora years ago. We failed then.”

“Does that mean we should simply surrender?” Master Piell sneered,
shaking his head. “No. I don’t know this Kronos that Tachi wishes us to
save, but we have a responsibility,” the tiny Master said firmly. “I say
we send Master Gallia a message, and I myself volunteer to go to Utapau
immediately.”

“I agree,” Master Billaba nodded. “I will accompany Master Piell.”

Poof glanced around the room, wondering if there’d be any voices of
dissent. Instead, he caught an odd look from one member in particular.
“Master Mundi?” he asked.

The Cerean Jedi’s features were scrunched up in thought. “Kronos… I
believe I’ve heard that name before.”

The Master’s brows furrowed, clearly trying to leverage the Cerean
species’s prodigious powers of recollection to their fullest before his
eyes snapped open in realization.

“Master Dooku!” he gasped. “I recall Master Dooku’s last report.”

Poof tried to rack his own memory at that, only to remember he hadn’t
actually /read /Dooku’s last report. The taciturn Master had been
investigating the supposed returned Sith for years now, searching for
the ones responsible for Qui-Gon’s death with no luck.

The latest report hadn’t been one he’d read directly; he’d been too busy
and hadn’t managed to catch up on it, trusting that if there was
something that was of note there, he’d learn of it through the Council
meetings.

“What do you recall?” he asked, head leaning forward on his long neck so
he might rest his chin on his hand.

“Master Dooku claimed he was getting close to the Sith and would be
hiring transportation. Kronos was a name he mentioned…”

“If that’s true, then it’s entirely possible the Bando Gora are aiming
to kill not just Kronos, but Dooku, as well,” Plo-Koon said. “There is
no need to debate further,” the Master said firmly. “We must act. If
Masters Billaba and Piell will proceed to Utapau, I will move
immediately to inform Master Gallia, Knight Kenobi and Padawan
Skywalker. Then, I will travel there myself, as well.

“Three Jedi Masters, possibly more, a Knight and a Padawan…” Poof
balked, just a bit, knowing that Kenobi and Skywalker /would/ be going
headfirst into danger immediately, of course).

That was… a significant level of fighting strength for one mission.

“The last time the Jedi battled against the Bando Gora, we had nearly
double that number,” Piell pointed out. “We still failed to bring them
down.”

Poof hesitated, unsure in his decision without Masters Yoda or Windu
here to give their approval, but eventually, he sighed. It would be
worse if he did not act.

“Very well,” he nodded. “May the Force be with all of you.”

Masters Piell, Billaba and Plo each stood from their seats, bowing
towards the Council before immediately marching out the door to prepare
for their mission with all due haste.

_/*Chapter 35:* / _

 

_/*Bail Organa. * / _

This… was not a call he’d expected to have a month ago. Hell, a week
ago, he hadn’t expected to have this call.

Just this morning, he figured he perhaps imagined it as some sort of
fever dream.

But… no. This was certainly happening.

You couldn’t blame him for his disbelief. Satine was a good woman, but
her stance on pacifism was… extreme, even by Alderaanian standards.

This act was very much unlike her, and skirted the possibility, if not
the /probability,/ of very real violence on the proverbial horizon.

“I must admit,” he began somewhat hesitantly, a holoconference call
arrayed across his desk in front of him. “that, while I sympathize, I do
have some concerns, Duchess.”

“As do I,” the Diktat of Corellia, Aranos, chimed in. “I am willing to
support your efforts against slavery in the Outer Rim. I believe we,” he
nodded towards the other dozen heads of state, “are all in agreement
here on that, but what you’re talking about… it acts outside the laws of
the Republic.”

“Not entirely,” Satine answered, voice calm, posture straight and
poised. “The Republic does not directly regulate trade agreements
between sovereign planets so long as they abide by the core tenets of
the Republic Trade Charter. It is, after all, how the Trade Federation
has gotten away with so much recently.”

Many eyes darted towards the Naboo queen; the memory of the Trade
Federation’s blockade and invasion was still relatively fresh in many
minds. What happened on Naboo hadn’t sat well with many. The fact that
it was /legal/ even less so.

Seeing the attention drawn to her, Amidala - Queen for at least a
handful more years until her second term expired - spoke to Satine
directly. “Is this not premature?” she asked. “We have no reason to
believe the Republic would take issue with your rescue of slaves. Why
are you so convinced that they will seek to harm you economically that
you’d go to such lengths as to secure our economic aid preemptively?”

A fair question… if perhaps a naive one. He forgot so often that Padme
was so very young and idealistic.

The logic behind Satine’s actions was sound, and not at all premature.
There were /many/ Core Worlds that benefited from the slave trade.

If they formed enough of a power block that they could push through
sanctions… Mandalore would have no choice other than to almost
immediately reverse course on how they were dealing with Outer Rim
slavery and the Hutts.

“I concur with the young queen,” Orn Free Taa said, his rather
prodigious… /chins/… jiggling as he nodded. “Why not go through legal
channels? I am in full support of Mandalore’s desire to help my people
and end the Hutts’ slave trade, but not if it comes at the expense of
your good name and standing-”

“We are an Outer Rim planet, ourselves, senator,” Satine cut in easily.
“You all /know/ how I’ve worked to rehabilitate my people. Help them
move beyond their blood soaked past. The Hutts /actively/ undermine
those efforts, hiring Mandalorian mercenaries as enforcers, or as
soldiers in their crime wars..”

Her features darkened. “I would rather send them a message sooner,
rather than later: Mandalorians are no longer their pet kath hounds, to
be let loose whenever they wish something mauled. I /know/ the Republic
would wish for a far less… disruptive approach to these negotiations.
They cannot sanction the Hutts in a meaningful way to force them to
negotiate, but they can sanction Mandalore. I’d rather avoid such a
situation, especially given the inherent virtue we’re… trying to defend.”

/“‘Fighting,’/” Bail thought. /“That’s the word you’d rather not use.” /

He had to wonder what had changed. What part of Satine or Mandalore had
shifted recently that caused her to take up a /fight/.

Satine paused, taking a breath. “I am not seeking to circumvent
legality. Nor do I wish to cause anyone in this esteemable gathering
undue harm to their standing, but neither am I willing to let Hutt /
crime lords/ dictate to myself and others as though /they/ are masters
here. If Queen Amidala and Senator Taa are correct and the Republic will
support us, then this agreement is merely a formality. But if the Hutts
bully enough into believing their threats of open war that they’d take a
more cautious approach, my people would be grateful to know that we do
have allies in the Republic that understand and support us with more
than just words.”

She turned her attention onto Senator Taa. “I /know/ you, of all people,
Senator, will advocate on our behalf when the subject arises in the
halls of the Senate, and eventually you will convince that esteemable
body of the logic and righteousness of what we do, but, in the meantime,
how many more will be enslaved? How long will we languish in inaction?”

Very long. Bail had devoted his life to the Republic, to the Senate. But
he was not blind to the Republic’s many, /many/ flaws. Interminable
gridlock being one of them… especially when some put their minds to it.

Taa blushed, his cheeks darkening to purple rather than blue. “I, well,
of course, Duchess. I would wish nothing more than to support you,” he
nodded, and again, his chins jiggled. “And… it is, as you say, merely a
formality when the Republic supports you…” The Twi’lek’s jaw was set.
“Yes. I’ve decided. I will support this agreement. Ryloth will aid
Mandalore economically should they need it.”

An empty promise… Ryloth did not have enough economic strength to
support /itself,/ but it was a symbolic victory regardless.

The Diktat of Corellia, the First Secretary of Bothawui, and the
Director of Kuat each shared a look, an entire conversation passing
between the three before the Kuati director spoke.

“I will also agree to this measure,” he answered. Bail tried to reason
out why he might. Perhaps trade disruptions had lessened with the Hutts
hiring so many mercenaries and pirates to safeguard their slaves?

“Let it not be said that Corellia didn’t do its share to fight slavery,”
Diktat Aranos nodded. “We agree.”

“Bothawui agrees as well.”

One by one, the various leaders agreed or disagreed. Most fell in line
with the consensus. Only Balmorra and Ord Mantell wished to steer clear
of things.

“I still believe this is a premature stance… but the evil of slavery is
a blight on this galaxy. And I am willing to do my part to see others
freed,” Queen Amidala answered with a solemn nod. “I agree, and add
Naboo to your proposal, Duchess Satine.”

Finally, all eyes fell onto him. Alderaan was one of the most stable,
and economically prosperous, worlds in the galaxy. With his stamp of
approval, there would be no viable way the Republic could sanction
Mandalore significantly, not without making it politically… obvious
where they stood on the subject of slavery.

Thus, his own agreement, he was fairly sure, would render the entire
thing moot…

The senators who wished to stop the Duchess would need to find some /
other/ weapon, besides economics.

“Alderaan agrees,” he declared, nodding and offering the Duchess a
small, barely there smile, almost like a joke between old friends.

He was fairly sure she understood when she smiled back. Just a hint,
then it was gone.

“Thank you, sirs and ladies.” The Duchess bowed her head just a bit
where she sat.

—--------

On the other side of the line, as the conference call came to a close,
Satine let out a breath she hadn’t even known she was holding before she
opened her eyes to meet Alexandria’s gaze across her desk.

“It's done,” Satine said, her features scrunching up. “How did you know
Senator Taa would agree?” she asked. “I thought… well-”

“He’s a puppet,” Alexandria answered with a shrug. “Sending the ‘short
notice’ message didn’t give his puppet master any time to prepare or
give him marching orders. Taa himself, believe it or not, is actually
rather well meaning.”

Satine raised a rather /incredulous/ eyebrow. Senator Taa’s corruption
was… well known… by /everyone/. “You’re not serious.”

“He’s just /incredibly/ stupid,” her advisor shrugged again. “Still.
That task was pivotal. With our finances secure we can push towards the
next stage.”

Satine’s lips pursed. “And that would be?”

“Get clan Wren onto Ryloth.”

_/*Taylor:* / _

“The seditious elements were rounded up and dealt with most effectively.
Forgive me for saying this, but from previous missions undertaken with
your order, such a thing is unusual for Jedi,”

“These separatists were planning to cause significant harm to your
planetary security forces. As such, we deemed that there was sufficient
cause to engage with a higher level of force than normal.”

It was a willow, thin man that spoke to Master Windu.

His name was Tarkin.

Former military, a politician now, assigned by someone, somewhere, to

Apparently, we’d dealt with the problem before he could arrive.

Which, according to what I’d heard from my bugs across the building,

Impressed because, as he said, he hadn’t thought we’d act so… decisively.

And irritated because now his report would be far less detailed when he

‘I showed up and the insurgents were already dealt with,’ wasn’t quite
as impressive as the alternative, after all.

“I’m hardly complaining, Master Jedi,” the man answered drolly. “Merely

/Or desperate/. I thought, but didn’t say. I knew better than most;
