His heart stirred in excitement, pleased at the very thought.

It would be soon. Very, very soon.


    Chapter 58: Interlude: Year Six

_/*Interlude: Year Six* / _

_/*Taylor*/_:

I do love Kashyyyk.

I’ve said it before, I know, but I’ll say it again.

The Wookiees were always kind, always helpful, and willing to open their
doors.

When I recognized that what I had come here to do was going to become a
regular /thing/ and that the Jedi temple couldn’t really accommodate it
with everyone’s safety in mind, the first people I’d thought to ask had
been the Wookiees.

They’d been happy to help.

It was so rare to find people like this, and I couldn’t help but love
them for it.

The insect life on Kashyyyk was just a bonus, no matter what Vicky said.

My hand patted Atlas II’s side fondly, the vibration of his rapid
wingbeats thrumming underneath me. He’d grown since I last saw him.
Large enough now to lift a fully grown Wookiee. I’d heard Attichitcuk
rode him into battle against a slaver raid just a few months ago while
we were offworld; plenty of Wookiees commented how he was strong enough
to tear gunships apart.

I must’ve looked laughably small on his back, but the bug’s mind hummed
with a peaceful sort of calm as I controlled him, recognizing the
sensation from when he’d been little more than a hatchling.

A hatchling that’d been the size of a decent sized pony, but that was
Kashyyyk.

Up ahead I could see the elevated dais, built on a platform resting on
the twisted and bent branches of the tallest wroshyr trees. We were
miles away from the village. Vicky would have come with me, she usually
did, but she’d been tired. Master Billaba had asked her to help design a
combat lesson plan for the Knights training in the Shadowlands to fight
Sith. Vicky could be devilishly clever while knowing just how far was
‘too far’, a skill I didn’t share when it came to combat training. I
always felt it was better to hit them as hard as you could in training,
because they could /get up/ if they fucked up in training. Less so on
the field.

But I’d been overruled by damn near everyone on the Council. I wasn’t
surprised. Nor bitter.

Even so, Vicky had been up almost all night with Master Billaba,
brainstorming, so I wanted to let her sleep.

And it was good to ride on Atlas II again. Big as he was.

We descended, the large can-cell’s spindly, hooked legs touching down on
the platform like a helicopter, its wings folding back before I made
them rise straight up so I could dismount.

I offered the bug a scratch along the center of his forehead, between
the eyes, its primitive mind almost purring in pleasure at the sensation
before I turned him around and sent him off to graze and eat some of the
fruits hanging off the tree branches directly below us.

I took a deep breath, marching into the center.

The Wookiees had decorated the structure, paints of bright yellows, bone
whites, muddied reds and vibrant greens swirled and whorled at my feet
in splashes of color that offset the dull bark of the wroshyr tree wood.
Part shamanism, part wood treatment, so the structure wouldn’t rot. It
was strangely fitting. Yoda, Yaddle, Billaba and Windu frequented this
place for their own private meditations sometimes.

There was a small little ‘tent’ at the edge of the platform, something
that held supplies, a first aid kit, and an emergency communicator just
in case, but beyond snacking on the occasional candy bar I don’t think
it’d ever really been used by anyone.

I took another deep breath, reaching the center of the platform where
all the paints met in a great, spiraling tapestry.

I placed the mat I’d brought with me first: one experience with raw
knees and shins had been more than enough for me to learn my lesson.

Kneeling down, I settled in, taking one last deep breath before the plunge.

I opened my mind.

The mat disappeared, the wooden platform followed after it. The trees,
the wildlife, the gentle hiss of leaves in the breeze, the creaking of
swaying branches, the trilling hoots of distant apes, the wingbeats of
birds and scuttling lizards.

One by one, like stars winking out in the night sky, they vanished.

I felt /her,/ then. Moving, /coalescing/, a titanic swell, like an ocean
in a storm surge descending, only /so much more/.

Vicky didn’t need to do this. She could commune with the Fragile One
almost whenever she wished. It was smaller, simpler. Like one of our
kids even as it was more alien. It was happy to help, to be of help, and
it tried with far greater ease to connect with Vicky’s wants and needs.

It wasn’t the same for the Queen Administrator, even as I /knew/ that
she /was/ trying.

It hurt. Even now it /hurt/ to focus on her, to try and even remotely /
grasp/ the enormity of /her/.

The storm moved around me; stars collapsing, suns blotting out, endless
voids of dark, collapsing matter as she continued to /try/.

Slowly, bit by bit, piece by piece, like water droplets gathering at the
basin through thin channels.

I felt her /become/.

I’d asked her once, only once, why. Why did she want this? What did she
hope to get out of it?

Her answer had been ‘simple’, the concept thrown at me as the Passengers
spoke to each other, databombs that someone like me could only scramble
to pick up the smallest edges of.

_/*“Understanding.”* / _

I had pressed further. “Why?”

She’d tried, then. /Tried/ to put it into words. Forced herself to do
things /this /way.

/‘Experience… Symbiosis -Greater than- Parasitic. Possibilities.
Expanded. Infinite. You. Infinite.”/

And that was a whole different kind of scary.

To have expectations, /idealized/ expectations, from something that
viewed you as being able to give it ‘infinite’ possibilities.

It was terrifying.

But I tried. I made myself try, the same way she was making herself try.

Because if I could infuse one single atom of understanding, one /
molecule/ of what it meant to be /human/… then maybe when I was gone,
Khepri wouldn’t ever happen again. That she’d know how to use that
power, those /infinite possibilities/ to make it easier on the /next/
person she chose. And maybe that person could help her further.

Bit by bit. Piece by piece.

She wanted to understand, to grow. Like she had before. I wanted her to
understand so that /when/ she grew, not /if/, she’d still stand by the
conclusion she’d already reached. That symbiosis, mutual cooperation,
was /better/ than consuming us, leeching off us. It didn’t /have/ to be
the way the Warrior set things up to be.

So I waited now, focusing, even as my brain throbbed with pain, sensing
the whole of her collapse, fold in on itself, until, instead of /
worlds,/ I sensed nothing but a single mote of /dust/.

I opened my eyes.

She stood there. Stardust and starlight shining incandescently in front
of me, the form struggling to maintain itself, flickering at the edges,
tiny shards of glass breaking apart, hovering around the main body
before slipping back into place with bursts of rainbow light.

I breathed, taking in the sight.

_/*“Hello.*/_”

The voice was /loud/, like someone screaming through a thousand
megaphones at once. It wailed and screeched, a high note sending a
needle of pain through the back of my teeth as I winced.

The form distorted a bit more, distressed.

But still, it was a /word/, something said with a /voice/.

“You’ve been practicing,” I noted.

The distortions eased, warmth suffusing me. She wasn’t speaking but
through the Force, our connection, I could sense her appreciation that
I’d noticed.

_/*“Understanding. Greater,”*/_ She preened, proud. _/*“More data
required. Greater understanding needed. Further results achievable.”*/_

I… well, /understood/ what she was getting at. She needed more time,
more practice.

I nodded, offering a smile as best I could. “You’ll get there,” I commented.

She shimmered, breaking and reforming. Joy.

Then, unexpectedly, she held out her hand, a shimmering light on her palm.

_/*“Understanding,*/_” she said, holding it out further. _/
*“Understanding!*/_” she insisted, eager and excited.

I hesitated for a moment, old fears that I hadn’t quite cured myself of
coming back before I steeled myself.

I reached out, my fingers brushing against the glimmering, shining
surface of a star.


    Chapter 59: Chapter 47

_/*Chapter 47:* / _

_/*Anakin:* / _

It was very rare for Anakin to /rush/ anywhere. Oh, sure, he would
happily… borrow a starfighter or any ship he could get his hands on and
test the engine’s max speed limit to get somewhere ‘on time’, but that
was for fun. That was different.

Rushing implied /urgency/, a /need/ to get somewhere as fast as
possible, not just an inane /want/.

So yes. He – typically carefree, easily amused and rather irreverent
Anakin Skywalker, the ‘Chosen One’ – rarely /rushed/ anywhere.

But he was doing so now.

The guards were clustered around the hall of the Sundari Royal Palace.
As soon as he drew close, one readied their weapon with a glare and
Anakin hastily brought his hands up to show he was no threat.

“Lower your weapon, Naboo,” Aras’ voice rumbled out of his helm, a
gauntleted hand grasping the Naboo guard by the vambrace “This one is a
friend.”

The Naboolian royal guard didn’t look happy, but even so, he did lower
his weapon.

Aras nodded. “Skywalker.”

“Aras,” Anakin breathed, letting himself catch his breath after
sprinting across half the palace. “What happened?”

“An assassin,” the massive man who’d taken Anakin’s own mother into his
home answered with a grim sneer curling his lip. “A successful one.”

Anakin felt his heart drop, the hallway spinning for a moment before he
stumbled forward. Aras didn’t stop him as he moved past him and the
other Mandalorian, Naboolian and Alderaanian guards.

The inside of the room was far less crowded than its exterior, likely
due to its much greater size; the hall felt cluttered, claustrophobic.
But this room, with its wide open spaces and high ceiling felt almost
airy, even if every corner was stuffed full of more guards.

In the center of the room, with Master Fay kneeling at its side – a body.

“Padme!” he didn’t recognize his own voice at first, his heart leaping
up to his throat even as it fell down to his feet.

He rushed forward, his eyes fixed on the pretty, painted corpse of the
former Naboo Queen, now a Senator, the girl he felt as though he’d loved
since the moment he laid eyes on her.

He could see the wound that had ended her life, still smoking, charred
flesh and cloth around its edges. A lightsaber slash.

Then, Obi-Wan was there, his Master standing in his way but Anakin
couldn’t hear him. His voice sounded distant, almost underwater. He
struggled, ready to push past his Master to reach Padme even as Obi-
Wan’s hands grasped at his shoulder

“Ani-”

The voice cut through the fog – as long as it had been, as many years as
had rolled by he /knew/ that voice.

His head whipped around, fixing immediately on one of the four
handmaidens sitting off to the side, many of them crying. Padme, the
real Padme, staring right at him was crying and it was so good to see /
that/ and not…

His eyes turned back, looking over Obi-Wan’s shoulder to the corpse.

A double.

Of course… a double.

It’d been how he met her… and here it was again.

The relief felt like water rushing across his body, its cool kiss
quenching the fires of desperation, fear and anger.

“Padme?” he called hesitantly, almost cautiously.

She offered a hesitant, tremulous smile in return, the tears still
marking her cheeks.

“Not many know-” Anakin turned to the voice, finding a man he distantly
recognized as the Senator of Alderaan, Bail Organa. “Outside of our most
private guards. So let's keep this quiet, Master Jedi, please.”

“What happened?” he finally found it in himself to ask, turning to look
at Obi-Wan.

Master Fay stood, the eddies of the Force that had been flowing from her
into the body, either in an attempt at healing or some other ritual
performed by the Sephi Jedi Master.

“A Sith,” the woman whispered, breathing deeply.

Anakin felt his heart again jump in his chest. “You’re sure?”

“I’ve given the best description I could,” Satine finally spoke up. “I…
I’m almost certain it was a woman. Twin red blades.”

“Almost certain?” he pressed.

“A holofield,” Obi-Wan explained, gesturing to his wrist for emphasis.
“Worn on the wrist, she looked like Arisa. The guards are checking her
quarters now. We’re /hoping/ she’s just knocked out, not dead, but…” his
master shook his head. “It’s not looking good.”

Arisa had been a serving girl; he knew her. She always smiled for him
and Obi-Wan, even brought him honey for tea once when he confessed he’d
never tried any.

His gaze flicked from Padme, to Organa, to Satine. “None of you were
unprotected. Were without your guards,” he shook his head. /Trying/ to
focus, to pull together the panicking fragments of his mind to
something /coherent/. Something that could be useful. “She must have
known she’d have only one shot at this, before she’d be swarmed.”

Anakin turned his eyes towards the far window, shattered into a million
pieces. He knew these high rise window panes were shatter proof, unless
exposed to something extreme, like the heat of a lightsaber.

Then he looked towards the floor, where a massive /hole/ had been formed
by /something/.

Obi-Wan must’ve noticed his look, his Master beginning to explain.

“Satine was the one who noticed something was wrong,” he began with a
nod towards the Duchess who sat slumped in her seat, forehead cradled in
her shaking hand. “Arisa always…” he hesitated, clearing his throat.
“She always smiled, greeting the Duchess with a good morning or a good
evening.”

“This time she just bowed…” Satine cut in. “/Duchess/,” she mimicked.
“Didn’t even look at me.” The blonde woman shook her head. “The more I
watched, the more I knew something was wrong. I pressed my personal
alarm,” she gestured towards a gemstone necklace, or at least what /
looked/ like a gemstone necklace.

Anakin knew the system. One tap for the guards to be on alert. Two for
immediate intervention needed, and three for a flat out emergency.

“The Sith,” Obi-Wan continued, “must’ve sensed something was wrong. She
struck before she was ready.” He gestured towards the body.
“Unfortunately… Alexandria hadn’t made it in time to avoid all casualties.”

“Alexandria?” he echoed, curious. He knew that Alexandria was a
parahuman, but her abilities were something of a mystery next to the
others. He’d never /seen/ her abilities.

He turned his eyes towards the hole in the floor. Victoria could have
done something like that. Could Alexandria do the same?

Obi-Wan nodded. “The Sith ran, her holofield turning into a cloaking
field. The guards and Alexandria are tearing the palace apart right now.”

Anakin shook his head. “I can’t sense her.”

“None of us can,” Fay said, the beads and charms on her golden hair
swaying with the shake of her head. “This assassin has mastered the
ability to hide her signature. Even nearby, I never once felt her.”

That… that was dangerous.

Anakin remembered the Sith woman on the asteroid so many years ago, that
radiating aura of rage and hate. To think it could be hidden, that it
could be /silent/ until it was too late… a disquieting notion.

“Should we join the search?” he asked.

“No. We need to stay with the Duchess and the Senators,” Obi-Wan said,
nodding once in Padme’s direction.

“Why? The assassin is hiding, we might be able to sense her or at least
help if we’re close enough?” he asked.

“Think, Anakin,” Obi-Wan said, not unkindly. “The assassin had to act
before she was ready, so we can’t be sure if Senator Amidala was her /
actual/ target, or if instead it was Senator Organa or the Duchess, and
Senator Amidala’s handmaiden was sadly caught in the crossfire.”

That… that was a good point.

“I already have several Knights of the enclave joining the search,” Fay
volunteered. “So I agree with Master Obi-Wan. It would be best if we
stay with these three, you two in particular are the greatest combatants
the enclave has available at the moment.”

“And so we must act as bodyguards,” Obi-Wan finished for her.

Anakin nodded, mentally dismayed (again) at Master Fay’s stance on
pacifism. He could /feel/ the woman’s overwhelming mastery of the Force.
If she had even a little inkling towards combat, she could easily be one
of the strongest combatants in the Order.

“I will remain with the Duchess,” the woman said calmly, “I imagine
Alexandria will do the same once she returns. As such, my weakness in
combat will not be an issue.”

Obi-Wan nodded. “Then I shall remain with the Senator, if you have no
objection, Senator Organa.”

“Not at all,” the Alderaanian forced a smile onto his face, still drawn
tight with tension and jittery nervousness.

Obi-Wan offered a firm nod. “Then you, Anakin…” he nodded towards Padme,
“Will remain with Senator Amidala for now.”

The boy felt his heart /again/ flop in his chest.

Even so he turned, offering a smile towards the woman who was so very,
very fortunately alive.

“I’d be glad to, Master,” he answered.

—

Hours later, long after the sun had fallen, the palace was a home turned
into a /fortress/. There were checkpoints at every junction, guard
checks at each elevator station. Alexandria had taken over the palace
security, and Anakin could tell she was leaving /nothing/ to chance.

Two senators dying in Mandalore’s own palace on a diplomatic visit?

If the Sith had been successful, it might very well have been the /end/
of the Coalition the Vizier had spent so many years and a lot of
political influence constructing.

A single /instant/ of carelessness had nearly cost them everything.

No, he couldn’t blame her for the extra security, tedious as it might
have been.

Even so, they couldn’t stay at their charges’ side every second of every
day. Eventually, they had to report these events to the Council, that
the Sith had made their move.

_/*“This news is… concerning*/_.”

Master Windu’s understatement belied the growing concern Anakin could
see forming on the Jedi Master’s face. His eyes were not even really
looking at him, Fay or Obi-Wan, but rather rapidly darting this way and
that way as his mind pieced together just how close they’d come to
complete disaster.

/“If either Senator Amidala or Senator Organa would have truly fallen,
the anti-slavery Coalition may have collapsed. It would have left
Mandalore alone, isolated politically,” /Master Ki-Adi-Mundi said.

/“And able to be attacked by its enemies, including the Hutts… it would
have been war,” /Piell sighed, his one good eye clenching shut as he
shook his head. /“What a mess/.”

/“I’m afraid it’s even worse than that,” /Master Trebor cut in. /“If one
of them would have been slain by a /Sith/, to many beyond our walls,
Sith are just another form of Jedi, or something that only exists in
history books. The public, and especially the Mandalorian public, would
have seen it as a Jedi attacking diplomats, even worse, the ruler of
Mandalore. Our Enclave there may very well have been attacked by
outraged Mandalorians if something had happened to the Duchess, and
public sentiment in the rest of the Republic worlds would have been
little better.”/

Anakin hadn’t considered that. It made for a grim thought.

/“We never should have placed an enclave on that world,” /Piell
muttered, his voice carrying easily.

/“The Sith cannot be allowed to succeed,” /Mace called, leaning back in
his seat. /“Many Masters are away right now, leading their enclaves, but
I will send a general call… and we will be assigning teams of two to
each potential target.”/

“Six Masters?” Obi-Wan’s voice carried the very real undercurrent of
shock. “That’s… unheard of for guard duty.”

/“If the Sith succeeds in killing any of those three at this juncture,
the damage it will cause will be catastrophic/,” Ki-Adi answered. “/An
overabundance of caution in this instance is better than carelessness.”/

“I understand-” Obi-Wan nodded. “-but even so, with the Conclave on
Corellia just a few weeks away it’s just… surprising.”

/“It is… a concern,” /Master Trebor admitted. “/But let us worry about
the Conclave, Knight Kenobi. Your primary concern now needs to be the
safety of your charges.”/

/“A moment, Masters,/” Master Rancisis said, holding up a hand as the
other stroked his long beard. /“Discretion might be needed here,”/ he
said. “/The Sith believes she killed one target. I see no reason to
undermine that belief. Two Masters returning with the Naberrie entourage
to Naboo will reveal her survival clear as day.” /The serpentine Master
gestured towards the two of them. /“I propose that we instead send
Masters as intended to Senator Organa and the Duchess of Mandalore, but
only Master Obi-Wan or Padawan Skywalker, not both, should accompany the
surviving Naberrie. They have been acquaintances since the Trade
Federation Crisis on Naboo. It would not be odd for at least one to
accompany her remains to pay respects.”/

Also a very good point, and a decent idea. Anakin itched to step
forward, to volunteer immediately, but… if it came down between him and
Obi-Wan, maybe Obi-Wan would be the stronger of the two of them to
defend her-

“Anakin has my full confidence.”

The words nearly bowled him over, and Anakin found himself whipping his
head around so fast towards Obi-Wan beside him, he felt the bones of his
spine crick.

/“He’s still a Padawan,”/ Piell commented.

“Not for much longer,” Obi-Wan said with a nod. “He is stronger than I
was at his age, and has been assisting in training /Knights/ in the
Shadowlands for years for an encounter with the Sith,” his Master
nodded. “As I said, he has my full and complete confidence. He can be
trusted with this mission and any mission you place before him.” Obi-
Wan’s hand came up, clapping Anakin on the shoulder as he finally turned
to look at the stunned youth with a small, barely there smile on his
bearded face. “I can remain here on Mandalore, and his absence will be
far less conspicuous than my own anyway.”

/“Hmmm.” /The sound Mace released was contemplative, eyes like knives as
he stared through the hologram.

For the first time in a while, Master Fay’s voice cut in, stopping Mace
from speaking.

“I agree with Knight Kenobi,” the woman nodded, offering a small smile
in Anakin’s direction. “The Force urges us to accept this course of action.”

The other Masters exchanged glances. Mace leaned back in his seat,
fingers interlaced in front of him. /“We will consider this approach and
give you an answer soon. In the meantime, keep the Senators and Duchess
safe and on Mandalore for now. You can expect the Masters to arrive in
just a few days. The VIPs *must *stay on the planet under extreme guard.
The Sith cannot be allowed to kill any of them.”/

“I understand, Master Windu,” Obi-Wan bowed, Anakin following suit,
sensing the conversation was over.

Mace nodded./“Padawan, Knight, Master,” /he said to each of them in
turn, nodding before the feed was cut off leaving the room in gloomy
darkness.

—

“Mom,” Anakin was /not/ whining. “I’m fine, really!”

His mother cupped at his cheeks, turning his head this way and that way.
“You don’t look like you’ve been eating,” she chided… as she always did
when he came to visit.

He didn’t always come. Sometimes, he guiltily had to admit, he tried not
to. He knew very well the fact that he visited his mother was a secret
Obi-Wan was keeping for him and he didn’t want to abuse that. Most Jedi
didn’t get to see their parents.

But after today, with Padme nearly dying… and Arisa /likely/ having been
killed, well…

He just wanted to make sure.

“UNCLE ANI!”

The scream of joy brought a smile to his face and Anakin turned at the
sound of pounding feet rushing to meet him. He knelt down, grabbing hold
of the little boy that was, in truth, getting to be not so little anymore.

But he was still small enough Anakin could pick him up with a dramatic
roar of triumph; the boy’s toy vibro-sword nearly smacking him in the
head as he did.

The now… six? Was it six? Or seven? S/ithspit,/ he was bad at remembering.

Either way, the boy laughed, delighted as Anakin twirled him through the
air before setting him back down. “Daryan!? Is that you! I didn’t
recognize you! You’re getting to be as big as a Wookiee!”

“I’ll be as big as dad when I grow up!” the boy declared proudly. Anakin
doubted it, but wished him the best of luck. Aras’ height was /not/ common.

“Hi, Uncle Ani,” Jen called, far more calmly as she walked in behind her
brother, dragging a stuffed doll of what Anakin guessed was a Basilisk
war droid behind her.

It wasn’t lack of enthusiasm that had her dragging the thing, but rather
because it was almost as big as she was. She was quite determined to be
ready for the day she got her own Basilisk war droid.

Nevermind that her father said the droids were long since lost, Jen said
she’d find one and it would be hers.

Anakin very much got the impression that the universe would bow to her
will… /or else./

He smiled at the twins, opening up his arms. “Where’s a good hug and
kiss for your uncle Ani, huh?”

Daryan lurched forward, nearly bowling him over before Jen walked into
her half of the embrace – it was a little awkward, hugging both her and
the basilisk plushie, but he managed.

Standing with the two twins in his arms was a bit of a struggle. “Ohhh,”
he groaned, smiling back at his softly smiling mother. “You want to feed
me like them, huh? They’re getting /huge/.”

“Children grow,” she said fondly “Much as we might want otherwise.” She
frowned then. “I heard there was some trouble.”

His own smile slipped. “Something like that… but… it’s fine,” he
assured. “We’ll deal with it.”

“Skywalker-”

/“Dad!/Daddy!”/

The two little ones squirmed out of his grip, rushing to get to their
father who marched in behind him.

Anakin offered a nod to the larger man, watching as Aras patted the
happy tykes on the head as they hugged at his legs, barely reaching past
his knees.

He looked at the older man. “Any developments?”

“None,” the palace guard answered. “Shift change.”

Anakin nodded. “And Miss Hannah?”

“With Cook,” he answered simply. “They’ll be returning in three days.
I’ve been told you might be leaving soon.”

Word spread fast. “That’s not confirmed yet.”

Another nod and a grunt, the door closing behind the man as he
extricated himself from the little ones, who still grabbed at his hands
or the cloth of his pants.

“You’re welcome here for your stay, if you wish,” he answered easily,
marching past him.

“Thank you, but I have a job for now,” he admitted. “I just came for a
short visit.”

His mother looked sad, but she understood. She always did. “Well, let me
get you some food to take with you.”

“Mom, I-”

“Shh. You’ll be taking food,” she declared. “We have too much.”

Aras grunted, but Anakin got the impression he didn’t /dare/ contradict
Shmi Skywalker when she wanted to give her son some food; so he stayed
quiet.


    Chapter 60: Chapter 48

_/*Chapter 48:* / _

_/*Vicky:* / _

 

The Jedi, much as she may have liked them, were not known for their
adaptability.

As much as she might have wanted otherwise, the Jedi response to rapid
change was typically to balk, or at best offer hesitant caution before
tepidly trying to navigate whatever change had come about.

Which kind-of explained the current situation rather well if she were
being honest.

“It is clear that her teachings are not appropriate for crechelings! I
daresay they’re barely appropriate for /any/ in our Order!”

The outraged declaration came from Saesee Tiin, and Vicky tried not to
glare at the Iktotchi Jedi Master from her place near the entrance of
the chamber.

He was through holo, so she was sure he couldn’t really see her at this
distance, but she hoped he felt the heat of her glare anyway.

“You are being unfair, Master Tiin,” Master Billaba called through her
own holo-channel. There were more holo-attendees than flesh and blood
ones, truth be told. The various enclaves demanded their respective
Masters be present, and the low number of High Council Masters was being
keenly felt more and more as time went on. “Knight Hebert has been
instrumental in our own training to prepare for the Sith on Kashyyyk,
and her perspectives are not without their merit.”

“There is no ignorance,” Master Plo quoted calmly, also on holo. “It is
a brittle belief that cannot suffer questions or contestation, Master Tiin.”

Tiin shot a heated glare Plo’s way, but before he could say anything,
Master Mundi cut in.

“The issue does not lie with /questions,/ Master Plo,” The Cerean said.
“It lies with her, spreading her personal beliefs onto young,
impressionable minds. She was not raised as a Jedi, she can be forgiven
for there being gaps in her knowledge, but if she means to continue
teaching crechelings, those deficiencies cannot be allowed to harm the
most vulnerable amongst our ranks. I worry Knight Hebert is letting her
personal feelings affect her teachings too much.”

“I am /well aware/ of my deficiencies, Master Mundi. Can you say the same?”

Taylor’s voice cut through the room like a knife, dark figure standing
tall and proud in the center of the Council Chamber. Master Mundi
furrowed his brows, Vicky could see it all the way from here even
through the glow of the holo that made up his form. Vicky felt torn
between smirking in petty satisfaction or groaning in dismay at Tay’s… /
Tayness/.

And people said /she /was a bad diplomat!

Clearly none of those people had ever been in a room with her girlfriend
‘playing nice’.

Mundi straightened where he sat, almost puffing himself up. “We cannot
have a Crechemaster who considers her personal teachings more prominent
than the fundamentals of what it is to be a Jedi.”

“Ask any one of my crechelings to recite the Jedi Code and they will do
so immediately,” Taylor countered.

“But a difference there is-” Yoda cut in, little legs crossed over his
seat, “-between knowing words, and understanding meaning.”

“Their Masters have half a lifetime to teach them their meaning of the
Jedi Code,” Taylor shrugged. “My job is to prepare them for what the
Jedi can’t teach.”

“And what pray tell is /that/?” Master Piel cut in, his one eye’s stare
piercing the girl in the center of the room.

“Things Jedi don’t consider. Things that don’t fall neatly into the
Code, things that don’t /fit/ that you can’t even see because of that
exact same reason.”

Many of the Masters, including some of their usual allies or at least
neutral parties, were looking more and more put off by the speech, if
not by her words then by the intensity which she delivered them, and
their detractors looked caught between anger and almost smugness that
Tay was just making their job of ousting her from the creche all the easier.

Luckily, before anyone could cut in, Master Plo offered Tay the lifeline
she needed, trusting that his erstwhile student had something to back up
her claims rather than just hot air.

“Such as?” The Kel Dor offered, his hand waving as if urging her to
continue.

“How many of you so very happily voted to send Siri Tachi off on that
multi-year infiltration mission with nothing but an objective and the
Jedi Code in her pocket?” Taylor immediately asked. Adi Gallia, went
completely pale at the words.

“She completed her mission.” Saesee Tiin argued. “And while her pain was
regrettable-”

“She was recovering /for years/ before she stepped foot outside of this
Temple again,” Taylor interrupted, grabbing hold of the momentum now and
refusing to let it go. “You didn’t prepare her better because you didn’t
have the tools to; you weren’t /looking/ for those tools either. Because
you’ve been so insulated for years with no outside opinions or ideas
that your teachings in the creche and the Masters afterwards are little
more than recycled, regurgitated platitudes.”

“Knight Heber-”

“How many of you thought to go retrieve Anakin’s mother from her
slavehood on Tatooine?”

Eeth Koth’s mouth clicked shut.

“Hmm?” Taylor pressed. “Did anyone not want to go for a day’s drive to
the Outer Rim to give your newest Jedi Padawan some peace of mind ten
years ago?” She shook her head. “You didn’t think of it because it
didn’t /fit/. A simple thing to do that wouldn’t have troubled you for
more than a week and a few credits that didn’t enter even the foggiest
corner of your mind because you don’t /think/ of things outside the
Code. My job is to make sure these kids /don’t have this flaw/. That
they learn to consider practical realities first, and the Code second.”

The Masters held their silence for a moment, many of them squirming
uncomfortably. Vicky knew for a /fact/ that many of them /hadn’t ever
thought/ of Shmi Skywalker, for many reasons. Some assumed /others /
would take care of it. Some assumed Qui-Gon had made arrangements with
the mother.

But not one of them had thought about or cared enough to ask. And for
generally good people like the Jedi, the knowledge that they’d been so
callous WAS deeply shameful on many levels.

Then the silence was broken when Ki-Adi-Mundi took a breath.
“Skywalker’s mother… was not a Jedi concern. While her situation was
deplorable, Tatooine is outside Republic jurisdiction, and it was an
attachment that needed to be severed as quickly as possible.”

Vicky couldn’t see Taylor’s face, but she could imagine her expression.
What she could notice was Master Koth’s eyes narrowing, displeased by
Master Mundi’s words.

“...As I said…” her partner answered in a voice so cold it could have
chilled the winds of Hoth. “I’m well aware of my deficiencies, Master
Mundi. /Can you say the same/?”

“Let us step back,” Master Windu cut in before the argument became truly
heated. The dark skinned master leaned back in his seat. “Knight Hebert.
Your knowledge base is not that of a traditional Jedi. This has proven
useful, as evidenced numerous times during our own training in the
Kashyyyk Enclave.”

Vicky nodded to herself. Good. That was a good sign. For all that Windu
was a traditionalist, he did try to give everyone a straight and fair shot.

“But I’m afraid I share some of my colleagues' concerns,” he said.
“Crechelings are not Jedi Masters. And while you /are/ correct in
pointing out recent errors and oversights in our judgment, I’m
uncomfortable with the thought that you would seek to /correct/ such
errors, on your own, by targeting young minds who know no better. Isn’t
this simply /your/ version of indoctrination? The same indoctrination
you accuse us of utilizing and stagnating into?”

Vicky winced.

/Shit/…

Her eyes swiveled around towards Taylor’s back, wondering how she was
going to argue this one.

Frankly, Windu was right; when Tay first laid out her plan, she /said/
as much straight to Vicky’s face.

Not for the first time, Vicky was reminded of the subtle manipulation of
the Council Chamber, the circular layout making one feel small and never
able to see all Masters at once. It was intimidating if you weren’t used
to it. Tay had a better edge than most with her bugs, but with two
thirds of the Council on holo that advantage was likely suffering.

Vicky had to wonder what exactly her girl was feeling right now. Her
mental shields were like an iron bulwark right now, so thick nothing was
getting in or out.

“These flaws can’t be fixed overnight,” Taylor said, standing still in
front of the Master, staring him dead in the eye. “Nor can I go to
individual Knights and Masters. You start at the foundation. It has to
be from the ground up, not from the top down. You all already have your
training, your ideas. You’ve acquired the experiences that have let you
square the Code with the realities of the galaxy around you. At best,
I’d just be preaching to the choir. At worst, talking to brick walls.”

Again, Vicky winced.

Seriously, how was /she/ the one with the reputation for being a bad
diplomat?

Filthy, slanderous lies!

“The kids are the ones learning /now/ to face the dangers of the galaxy,
and they need to be prepared for it. Things are /changing/ for the Jedi.
Enclaves across a half dozen worlds, some of them hostile or in hostile
zones. Clones who will be moving into active service under the Jedi /
next month,/ which is something none of /us/ had to deal with when we
were kids, unless I missed a memo somewhere…”

Some Masters did shift uneasily at that, the reminder that /yes,/ that
‘slave army’ that had been commissioned by Sifo was soon going to be /
their problem/ to manage.

“...The Hutts saber rattling across the Outer Rim, /more recruits/ than
ever being brought in, not only to the main Temple, but to the enclaves
as well, which means more diverse backgrounds, more diverse opinions and
schools of thought. Even more varied ages. The old status quo isn’t /
enough/.”

“And who’s fault is that!”

The outburst came from Saesee Tiin. The Iktotchi Master stood, horned
head framing a set of /furious/ eyes.

“For one thousand years our Order stood, strong and unchanging,
uncompromising in our beliefs, our values…” he shook his head. “Then,
suddenly, the two of you come along and seek to upend the established
order of things simply out of /convenience/! A girl who /stole
knowledge/ while sitting in our home as a guest, and another who
supports her every besmirching of our way of life without thought or
consideration. And now you want to use the children of a creche as your…
your /pieces /on the /board/! You go /too far!/

“Master Tiin.”

“No!” the Iktotchi protested over Master Windu’s call. “No,” he
repeated, more softly the second time. “You have allies on this Council,
but know that I am not one of them. When the day comes that your custody
of the creche will be decided, I will do everything within my power to
see you removed from your posting. Train Knights and others in the
bowels of Kashyyyk to your heart's content, but I won’t let a radical
like you taint the future of the Order.”

His piece said, he barely offered a curt “Masters” before departing with
a flicker of his holo image.

Tension had settled over the room, and one by one several of the other
Masters shut off their own transponders, leaving only Masters Yoda,
Windu and Gallia in flesh, along with the lingering Master Plo Koon.

“I will speak to him,” their old teacher said, his voice carrying that
same soothing calm it always did. “Change… does not come easily for Jedi.”

“No, Master,” Taylor said, turning to look at him. “You’ve done more
than enough. Don’t get caught in the fallout on my account.”

“You are still my student Taylor; it will never be any trouble. And I do
not think you’re incorrect.” His holo flickered off too.

Vicky saw Taylor’s shoulders sag, Windu and Yoda leaning closer to
whisper in each other’s ear as Adi stood from her seat to join them.

Her partner turned, walking out of the center of the room and towards
Vicky, who offered her a smile.

Vicky felt the sharp wave of relief, an undercurrent of joy and
gratitude that was juxtaposed by the expression on Taylor’s face.

“You shouldn’t be here,” she whispered, drawing close.

Vicky started: “I wasn’t gonna just leave you hanging out here /alone,/
Tay, screw that!”

She opened her mouth to protest and Vicky placed a single, /perfectly/
manicured finger against the bug controller’s lips, much to the
brunette’s clear, unimpressed irritation.

“I get it, you don’t want me caught in the splash zone. I appreciate it,
but it says it very clearly in the contract that I’m free to ignore you
when you’re being a well meaning idiot.”

Tay’s stare was absolutely /flat./

Vicky answered with a sunny smile.

Before the argument could go further, Masters Windu, Gallia and Yoda
began to approach. Vicky leaned over to peek past Taylor’s shoulder,
offering them each a smile and a wave.

“Hi,” she said, somewhat unnecessarily.

“Knight Dallon,” Windu nodded.

Taylor seemed to square her shoulders before she turned, facing the
three Masters before she crossed her arms. “I didn’t intend for it to
devolve into an argument, but I’m not apologi- ow.”

“Hmpf,” Yoda harrumphed, hobbling past her, his stick returning to its
primary function of helping him walk rather than rapping impertinent
Knights on their shins. “Say, you do, that conflict you did not wish,
but ever ready for it you are.”

“Truth be told, we did not /expect/ an apology,” Windu sighed, rubbing
at his forehead. “I do not agree with everything you said, but some of
it /did/ need to be said.”

“Oh?” Vicky tried not to perk up /too/ much at that, her eyes darting
over towards Taylor before darting back to the two Masters “That’s- ah,”
she paused, smiling as Yoda clambered up her back to find his usual seat
on her shoulder. “That’s… good?” she ventured.

Windu walked past her, “Walk with us, please,” he demanded and though
she and Taylor shared a curious look, did as they were asked.

The halls towards the Council Chamber were empty, but that wasn’t
unusual. Very few people needed to visit the High Council while it was
in session.

Even less so these days, when so many Jedi were off in wholly new
enclaves on so many other worlds.

“Some of us on the High Council have been speaking,” Windu began as they
reached the elevator. “And… after much meditation, we must admit that
we /are/ somewhat ill prepared for so many rapid changes.”

/That/ was not an admission she was expecting, nor was Taylor, judging
by the high arched brow she offered as the elevator doors slid open.

Windu stepped inside, Adi following after him. She and Taylor moved
quickly to follow.

“If you feel that way-” Taylor began. “-why the dog and pony show?”

Windu’s features scrunched up. “Pardon?”

Tay shook her head. “Sorry, turn of phrase from home,” she answered as
the doors closed. “I mean, why even meet with the others on the Council
at all regarding my teachings in the creche?”

“Because while we are in agreement that the Council is finding it
difficult to adapt to these changes…”

“That doesn’t mean we necessarily agree that /your/ methods are the best
solution. Or aren’t simply adding to the problem in less obvious ways.”

“Hmm.” Yoda nodded, his big ear tickling her temple. “Impacts, large and
small, our decisions have. Informed we must be of /all/ interpretations.
As much information as possible. The ideas of other Masters, in
opposition to you, valuable they are. As valuable as your own zeal for
your students.”

Vicky could understand that, even respect it. At least they were giving
Tay a /chance/ to say her piece in that regard.

Taylor crossed her arms. “Fair enough, I guess. But you’re not telling
me this for no reason.”

“No, we’re not,” Adi agreed, nodding.

“We’re telling you this so that you’re aware that the younglings in your
creche are the best form of advocacy you can convey, to myself and to
others who aren’t sure about your methods,” Windu said as the elevator
began its descent.

Adi spoke up. “It would be years before your students can demonstrate
their aggregate impact on the Jedi as a whole, and that change will not
be obvious or even traced back to you adequately.”

“So what are you suggesting?” Taylor demanded, her features scrunching
up as she tried to rapidly deduce what they were asking for and coming
up short.

“A conclave,” Yoda said. “On Corellia it will be held.”

“Yeah,” Vicky said, though in truth now /she/ was confused by the non-
sequitur, “but that’s, like, to decide who the next Masters of the
Enclaves are going to be, right? You’ll be assigning existing Jedi
Masters or ascending Knights to Masterhood so they can take up their
postings, right? At least, that’s what I heard,” she shrugged. “How does
that affect the younglings?”

“We believe you should take your oldest crechelings to that Conclave,”
Windu said.

Taylor blinked, the elevator coming to a stop with a lurch. “I… don’t
follow.”

Vicky was trying to piece it together, too. Glancing at Yoda in his
usual perch on her shoulder, and considering how the little gremlin
liked to do things, let her put two and two together.

“You want them to find Masters,” Vicky said.

Windu nodded, beginning to step out of the elevator and into the common
area. Many of the Jedi of all ranks offered respectful bows and
greetings before proceeding on their way.

“As I said,” Adi began, “it will be /years/ before we will truly know
the full extent of how your teachings affect us. But a selection of
students - older ones, who’s development we can see and measure more
proactively…”

“...will let you determine whether my methods are worth the pages
they’re written on,” Taylor summarized.

“It will at least be easier to do so,” Adi nodded gently.

“Many Masters and Knights, choose their Padawans by feelings in the
Force, they do,” Yoda nodded again. “If many of your students, chosen
they are…”

“Then it’ll give her some brownie points against the Masters that don’t
want her as Crechemaster.”

“It will at least give them pause,” Windu answered.

Taylor looked at the dark-skinned man and, just by the expression on her
face, Vicky very much wanted to cover Taylor’s mouth. A “bad diplomat”
moment was incoming!

But, alas, Vicky was too slow! And Yoda’s ear flicked her on the nose,
making her sneeze!

He did it on purpose!

“Why tell me this?” Tay asked. “You’ve always been a traditionalist,
Windu, and you weren’t exactly thrilled when I got my posting as
Crechemaster, so what changed? Why give me a leg up here?”

Windu turned his head, eying her. He was one of the few humans who had a
good two inches on Tay’s usual height advantage, which allowed him to
very convincingly put on an imperious stare when he wanted to.

“I wish for the Jedi to survive,” he answered succinctly. “The folly of
Dyas has cast a shadow across our name. Many in the galaxy call us
‘slavers,’ our Knights are rejected from setting foot on Republic
worlds, more and more there are whispers of war between us and the
Hutts, of Separatist factions looking to break away from the Republic
itself, and _/I,/_ as the Master of the Order, find myself…
overwhelmed. /Unprepared/,” his eyes turned towards Yoda on Vicky’s
shoulder. “I have help and wisdom in abundance to call upon, but I know
many other Jedi do not feel the same way in their postings.”

The man took a deep breath, turning and looking straight ahead. “As I
said, I’m unsure if you are the solution or merely another thing causing
instability. But I’m willing to… /try/ to give Padawans and younglings
more tools to face the galaxy that feels so very overwhelming these days.”

Vicky wasn’t sure what to say to that. She had the feeling Tay didn’t
either.

A feeling of… /responsibility/… a /weight,/ almost, felt settled on her
partner’s shoulders suddenly.

“Did that answer your question?” Windu asked.

“It did,” Taylor said slowly. ”Thank you.”

The man nodded. “Knight Hebert, Knight Dallon. Good day,” he said,
turning with a sharp face.

Adi and Yoda stayed behind.

“That was not easy for him to admit,” Adi said.

“No. It was not,” Yoda said. “But /better/ for it, he will be,” he
shifted on her shoulder, his stick booping her on the arm. “Come,” he
pointed with the end of the little WMD he flailed around in his tiny
tyrannical fist. “To the gardens we go.”

“Excuse me,” she laughed. “When did I become your taxi?”

“Indulge your elders, you will. Hmpf,” he said, haughtily.

“Fine, fine,” she acquiesced with another little laugh.

_/*Dennis:* / _

The winds /howled,/ whistling sharply, even through the thick, starship-
grade metal of the bulkhead.

The rains lashed down, a hissing pitter-patter on the steel and windshield.

The feeling that rose up in his stomach was strange.

He’d always liked storms. /Loved/ them even.

Then he remembered Leviathan.

And he felt guilty and stupid for ever liking storms. Storms killed
people, even when not being driven by a sentient force behind the wheel
of the natural disaster.

He sighed.

Rugess tapped him on the shoulder, babbling in concern.

He offered his best friend a smile. “I’m fine, buddy,” he said as he
reached over, picking up the mic for the intercom.

_/“Ladies and gentlemen, this is your captain speaking. We have
completed our landing and I’m pleased to inform you that we’ve reached
the greatest vacation planet known to the galaxy – Kamino. Where we have
sunny beaches and totally gorgeous alien women. It is not a flooded hell
hole, nor are the aliens very long, freaky looking fish people-”/ _

“Dennis!”

The scolding tone made him choke down a laugh that would have gotten him
in /so/ much trouble if he indulged it. “Sorry, /Mom,/” he drawled.

Hannah glared at him and a gloved hand smacked the back of his head, and
that /did/ make him laugh. Though not too hard. The /back/ of that hand
was still covered in beskar, after all.

The woman checked at her vambrace, which he knew was outfitted with a
sonar tac map and a motion tracker. /Just in case/.

“Be nice,” she demanded. “We’re just here to /assess/.”

“Yeah. Sure,” he nodded, standing up as he grabbed the belt with his
blasters, coiling it around his waist. “Just /assess,/” he repeated
drily. “Give ‘em a fair shake. You know, how they’re doin the same for
their clones. /Totally/ free-willed-and-eagerly-signing-up-for-the-army
clones.”

She glared at him, and he realized he wasn’t the only one with a whole
mixed bag of emotions here.

“I don’t like this, either,” she said. “But Satine and Alexandria trust
us to give them an honest assessment, so that’s what we’re going to do.”

He released a breath through his nostrils, almost huffing. “Fine.”

Stepping out of the cockpit, he turned to Rugess, “Don’t spool up the
guns, but keep ‘em primed just in case.”

Rugess offered a thumbs up.

Marching down the hall to the main living area and straight towards the
entry ramp, Dennis wasn’t surprised to find their last passenger already
waiting for them.

“Master Ti,” he nodded.

The Togruta Jedi Master turned, looking at him with a hesitant smile.

“Kronos,” she greeted, then offered a bow. “I would like to once more
express my sincerest thanks for your cooperation.”

He sighed, scratching at the back of his head. “Look, I get it. The Jedi
need a facelift right now and you guys getting a good photo op with a
famous slave liberator is gonna make a lot of people give you a second
chance. But I’ve told you already, I still haven’t even /seen/ how these
clones are being treated and until that happens, and I’m happy, I’m
not /cooperating/ with you yet,” he warned.

“I understand,” she assured, the picture of calm acceptance. “But even
so, you agreed to come here with me. You agreed to see for yourself
before forming your opinion. That’s more than most would do. Even if
nothing else comes of this I appreciate that, sincerely.”

Miss Militia stepped up behind him, beskar helmet hissing as it sealed
over her head. “You’re welcome, I guess,” he sighed.

The doors hissed open, and the ramp began to descend, letting in the
sound of the howling wind and hissing rain.

“Sunny beaches and gorgeous aliens, everybody,” he said drily, putting
on his own helmet before stepping out into the torrential downpour.

_/*Chapter 49:

Vicky:*/_

"Huh?"

Vicky wasn't often caught off guard, despite the somewhat exaggerated
persona of a carefree ditz. She was an observant and surprisingly shrewd
person when she chose to be. She /knew/ the people around her, and when
she didn't, she watched them /very/ carefully until she did.

But right now, in spite of all the years they'd known each other - in
spite of their rather close friendship with him - she stared at Yoda as
though the tiny green Master had just sprouted a second head. The slice
of fruit halfway to her mouth slipped from her fingers to fall to the
grassy dirt at her feet in her surprise.

Yoda's impish smile remained amused… but still sincere.

"Ok, ha ha, I get it," she said as her brain caught up, sucking a bit of
fruit juice off her thumb. "Funny, Green-Bean."

"Serious, I was being," said Green-Bean answered.

"I- No," she shook her head. "Uh-uh. I mean, /come on /– half your
Council is having conniption fits with Tay as a Crechemaster, and you're
seriously telling me to take on a /Padawan/?" She laughed again; the
sound emerging from her throat was forced and strained. "Tay's the
responsible one, here!" She was half lying, and they both knew it.
"She's the one that makes sure those kids do their homework and become
productive citizens. I take 'em out for ice cream and to play hookie!
Like… what?"

"And offer them hugs, when crying they are," he added. "Defend them from
bullies and callous words, you do. Always."

Looks like he wasn't gonna let her play the irresponsible 'get out of
jail free' card.

Vicky glared, stuffing the remains of the Kawa fruit into her mouth; she
could use the chewing time to think.

"You seriously want to rock the boat on this?" she pushed. "Now?
Freaking Tiin's gonna blow a gasket to the point his horns are gonna pop
off."

"Ready for this, you are," he insisted, utterly ignoring her very good
point. Ass.

"No, I'm not!" she said. "Green… Look, taking on a Padawan is basically
adopting a kid, and I'm not ready for that! I mean, yeah… my thirties
are sneaking up on me like a determined, inescapable serial killer, but
like… I'm not ready to be completely responsible for someone /else/,
turning them into a good person! That's…" she felt queasy. "That's
fucking terrifying. I haven't even talked about this possibility with
Taylor and I should do that for a big decision like this-" and she
should really shut up now. Shouldn't she shut up now? She should shut up
now. "I really should. You know. 'Cause she's my best friend and the
responsible one. No other reason." _/SHUT UP NOW, PLEASE!/_

Yoda reached up, grasping at her hand, and tugging her towards the
nearby bench.

Little Green hopped up onto the stone bench, patting the seat beside him
and Vicky allowed herself to sort of /plop/ down into it.

They lingered in silence.

"Look, if this is about convincing the other Masters on the Council
Tay's good for the job, I-"

"Not about Knight Hebert this is," Yoda shook his head. "About you.
Ready you are. Good you will be to a Padawan. Sense it, I do," he
declared, nodding firmly and smiling in a different way than the impish
prankster she so frequently plotted with. Nor the smug know-it-all that
dangled answers out of reach, nor even the indulgent grandpa watching
someone making a complete ass of themselves for his amusement.

It was the smile that promised that everything would be alright.

"Tied yourself, your actions and your wishes, to Knight Hebert you
have," Yoda said, and Vicky felt her heart stutter in its steady beat.

Was he saying…

"To help her in achieving her goals, your efforts have been," he
continued, easing the bit of worry. "A goal of your own, you must now
have. Your own growth, seen to. The next step, this is. Natural, this
is." He nodded with complete and absolute surety.

Vicky opened her mouth, closed it, then sighed, groaning as she rubbed
at her forehead, hoping the headache would /go away/. "I don't know,"
she answered. "I… I don't /feel/ ready. If the Force is supposed to
whisper in my ear to go to the creche. The creepy stalker/santa mix is
finally respecting the restraining order- Ow!"

The wack from the stick was reflex, familiar and comforting. Even as she
rubbed her arm from the impact she smiled; he did too.

The stick returned to its place on his lap… his hand was still gripping
it, though.

"Visit the creches you should," he nodded. "An answer, today you may not
find. Nor tomorrow. But ready for a Padawan, this I know you to be."

Vicky opened her mouth, ready to protest more when she decided against
it, her mouth clicking shut and shoulders slumping. "I… I'll think about
it?" she offered. He seemed so /sure/. It made her feel bad to break his
heart.

Her answer seemed to satisfy him, a happy nod and an affirming sound
escaping from his throat.

"Ow," she rubbed suddenly at the back of her hand. "What was that one
for?" she protested.

"Offer me Kawa fruit, you did not."

"You're /allergic,/ you little troll!"

"Gotten a different fruit you should have, then."
